q.p: Who is the performer of Doomsday (DC Comics)?
q.e: Doomsday (DC Comics): Sam Witwer. Doomsday is a supervillain appearing in American comic books published by DC Comics.

q.p: Who is the performer of Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe?
q.e: Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe: Édouard Manet. It depicts a nude woman and a scantily dressed bathing woman on a picnic with two fully dressed men in a rural setting.

q.p: Who is the performer of Ra's al Ghul?
q.e: Ra's al Ghul: Josh Pence. Stories featuring Ra's al Ghul often involve the Lazarus Pits, which restore life to the dying.

q.p: Who is the performer of O Captain! My Captain!?
q.e: O Captain! My Captain!: Meital Trabelsi. My Captain!" is an extended metaphor poem written by Walt Whitman in 1865 about the death of U.S. president Abraham Lincoln.

q.p: Who is the performer of Porgy and Bess?
q.e: Porgy and Bess: George Gershwin. It was adapted from Dorothy Heyward and DuBose Heyward's play Porgy, itself an adaptation of DuBose Heyward's 1925 novel Porgy.

q.p: Which company manufactures Tamagotchi?
q.e: Tamagotchi: Bandai. The original Tamagotchi, released locally in 1996 and worldwide in 1997, quickly became a major global toy fad for a period of time.

q.p: Which country is Café Terrace at Night from?
q.e: Café Terrace at Night: France. Café Terrace at Night is an 1888 oil painting by the Dutch artist Vincent van Gogh.

q.p: In which country is The Mousetrap?
q.e: The Mousetrap: United Kingdom. The Mousetrap is a murder mystery play by Agatha Christie.

q.p: Which country is The Treachery of Images from?
q.e: The Treachery of Images: United States. The Treachery of Images (French: La Trahison des images) is a 1929 painting by Belgian surrealist painter René Magritte.

q.p: In which country is The Last Supper (Leonardo)?
q.e: The Last Supper (Leonardo): Italy. The work was commissioned as part of a plan of renovations to the church and its convent buildings by Leonardo's patron Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan.

q.p: In which country is Socialist realism?
q.e: Socialist realism: Soviet Union. In visual arts, socialist realism often relied on the conventions of academic art and classical sculpture.

q.p: Which country is Girl with a Pearl Earring from?
q.e: Girl with a Pearl Earring: Netherlands. Girl with a Pearl Earring (Dutch: Meisje met de parel) is an oil painting by Dutch Golden Age painter Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665.

q.p: In which country was De Stijl?
q.e: De Stijl: Netherlands. De Stijl (Dutch: [də ˈstɛil]; 'The Style') was a Dutch art movement founded in 1917 by a group of artists and architects based in Leiden (Theo van Doesburg, J.

q.p: Which country is Pietà (Michelangelo) from?
q.e: Pietà (Michelangelo): Vatican City. It is a key work of Italian Renaissance sculpture and often taken as the start of the High Renaissance.

q.p: Which country is Come from Away from?
q.e: Come from Away: Canada. Come from Away is a 2017 musical, with book, music and lyrics by Irene Sankoff and David Hein.

q.p: Which country is Sonnet 18 from?
q.e: Sonnet 18: United Kingdom. The speaker then states that the Fair Youth will live forever in the lines of the poem, as long as it can be read.

q.p: In which country is The Garden of Earthly Delights based?
q.e: The Garden of Earthly Delights: Spain. The outer panels place the work on the Third Day of Creation.

q.p: In which country is Early Netherlandish painting?
q.e: Early Netherlandish painting: Burgundian Netherlands. It flourished especially in the cities of Bruges, Ghent, Mechelen, Leuven, Tournai and Brussels, all in present-day Belgium.

q.p: In which country is Laocoön and His Sons?
q.e: Laocoön and His Sons: Vatican City. The figures are nearly life-sized, with the entire group measuring just over 2 m (6 ft 7 in) in height.

q.p: In which country is Gothic art?
q.e: Gothic art: France. It spread to all of Western Europe, and much of Northern, Southern and Central Europe, never quite effacing more classical styles in Italy.

q.p: In which country is Shoes on the Danube Bank based?
q.e: Shoes on the Danube Bank: Hungary. The Shoes on the Danube Bank (Hungarian: Cipők a Duna-parton) is a memorial erected on 16 April 2005, in Budapest, Hungary.

q.p: Which country is What Did You Eat Yesterday? from?
q.e: What Did You Eat Yesterday?: Japan. What Did You Eat Yesterday? (Japanese: きのう何食べた?, Hepburn: Kinō Nani Tabeta?) is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Fumi Yoshinaga.

q.p: In which country was The Subtle Art of Not Giving a Fuck?
q.e: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a Fuck: United States. It was a New York Times and Globe and Mail bestseller.

q.p: In which country is Warsaw Ghetto boy?
q.e: Warsaw Ghetto boy: Poland. The exact location and the photographer are unknown, and Blösche is the only person in the photograph who has been identified with certainty.

q.p: In which country did The Death of Marat take place?
q.e: The Death of Marat: Belgium. Created in the months after Marat's death, the painting shows Marat lying dead in his bath after his assassination by Charlotte Corday on 13 July 1793.

q.p: In which country is Bocca della Verità?
q.e: Bocca della Verità: Italy. It still attracts many visitors who insert their hands.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Fluxus?
q.e: Fluxus: George Maciunas. Fluxus is known for experimental contributions to different artistic media and disciplines and for generating new art forms.

q.p: Which science fiction author is credited with coining the concept of a "positronic brain"?
q.e: positronic brain: Isaac Asimov. During his lifetime, Asimov was considered one of the "Big Three" science fiction writers, along with Robert A.

q.p: This Stephen King time-travel novel, his 60th published book, follows an attempt to prevent a presidential assassination and became a number-one bestseller — which novel?
q.e: 11/22/63 is a novel by American author Stephen King about a time traveler who attempts to prevent the assassination of United States President John F. Kennedy.

q.p: Published in three volumes in Japan between 2009 and 2010, this Murakami novel sold out on release day and topped a million copies within a month — which novel?
q.e: 1Q84 (Ichi-Ky-Hachi-Yon; stylized in the Japanese cover as "ichi-kew-hachi-yon") is a novel written by Japanese writer Haruki Murakami, first published in three volumes in Japan in 2009-2010.

q.p: A playwright by trade, this English writer found fame after a London Zoo visit where his son met a tame bear named Winnipeg — sparking a famous teddy-bear tale. Who was he?
q.e: A. A. Milne (18 January 1882 - 31 January 1956) was an English writer best known for his books about the teddy bear Winnie-the-Pooh, as well as children's poetry.

q.p: Anthony Burgess claimed he dashed off this 1962 novel in just three weeks, narrating teenage Alex's violent exploits in a Russian-flavored slang called 'Nadsat' — what is the book?
q.e: A Clockwork Orange (novel) is a novel by the English writer Anthony Burgess, published on 17 March 1962.

q.p: Beginning serialization in Kodansha's Weekly Shōnen Magazine in January 2020, this manga got two separate anime seasons — one in 2022, another in 2025 — which series is it?
q.e: A Couple of Cuckoos ("Cuckoo's Fianc(e)") is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Miki Yoshikawa.

q.p: Which Sarah J. Maas fantasy-romance series sweeps Feyre Archeron into the faerie lands of Prythian and an epic love story?
o: A Court of Thorns and Roses
q.e: A Court of Thorns and Roses is a fantasy romance series by American author Sarah J. Maas.

q.p: Split into two paperback volumes titled Dreams and Dust and After the Feast, this fifth book in an epic fantasy series topped bestseller lists in July 2011 — which novel?
o: The Fall of the House of Usher
q.e: A Dance with Dragons is the fifth novel of seven planned in the epic fantasy series A Song of Ice and Fire by American author George R. R. Martin.

q.p: Published in 1929 and set on the Italian front of World War I, this Hemingway novel about an American lieutenant and an English nurse became his first bestseller — which book?
q.e: A Farewell to Arms is a novel by American writer Ernest Hemingway, set during the Italian campaign of World War I.

q.p: Written and illustrated by Gido Amagakure, which manga ran in Good! Afternoon for three years before receiving simultaneous TV drama and anime adaptations in 2023?
q.e: A Galaxy Next Door is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Gido Amagakure.

q.p: Set mostly in New York City and following four friends through harrowing years of hardship, this acclaimed 2015 debut-length novel by Hanya Yanagihara is called what?
q.e: A Little Life is a 2015 novel by American writer Hanya Yanagihara.

q.p: Tennessee Williams' 1947 play follows faded Southern belle Blanche DuBois into her sister Stella's shabby New Orleans apartment — what is its title?
q.e: A Streetcar Named Desire is a play written by Tennessee Williams which was first performed on Broadway on December 3, 1947.

q.p: Barely noticed on its 1887 release, this Arthur Conan Doyle novel marked the literary debut of history's most famous detective duo — which book?
q.e: A Study in Scarlet is a detective novel by British author Arthur Conan Doyle.

q.p: Published as the follow-up to The Kite Runner, this 2007 Khaled Hosseini novel follows Mariam and Laila, two Afghan women bound to the same husband — which book is it?
o: The Fall of the House of Usher
q.e: A Thousand Splendid Suns is a 2007 novel by Afghan-American author Khaled Hosseini, following the huge success of his bestselling 2003 debut The Kite Runner.

q.p: This 19th-century Kazakh poet, composer, and philosopher pushed for cultural reform toward European ideas grounded in enlightened Islamic thought — who is he?
q.e: Abai Qunanbaiuly was Kazakh poet and composer (1845–1904).

q.p: Serialized for nearly a decade in Weekly Shōnen Magazine, this baseball manga got a 126-episode anime plus a sequel series still producing new episodes in 2026 — which title?
q.e: Ace of Diamond is a Japanese baseball-themed manga series written and illustrated by Yuji Terajima.

q.p: Regarded as Poland's greatest poet and one of its 'Three Bards,' this 19th-century Romantic writer is also considered a national poet in Lithuania and Belarus — who is he?
q.e: Adam Mickiewicz (24 December 1798 - 26 November 1855) was a Polish poet, dramatist, essayist, publicist, translator and political activist.

q.p: A student of the scholar Yusuf Hamadani, this 12th-century Sufi poet founded a mystical order that spread rapidly among Turkic-speaking peoples — who is he?
q.e: Ahmad Yasawi (1093-1166) was a Turkic poet and Sufi, an early mystic who exerted a powerful influence on the development of Sufi orders throughout the Turkic-speaking world.

q.p: This American play-by-play sportscaster called Monday Night Football for two decades before later calling Sunday Night Football for a rival network — who is he?
q.e: Al Michaels (born November 12, 1944) is an American television play-by-play sportscaster for Thursday Night Football and in an emeritus role for NBC Sports.

q.p: Hosting political broadcasts from 1970 through the 2000s, this veteran French commentator has also written for a major left-leaning daily since 1992. Who is he?
q.e: Alain Duhamel (French; born 31 May 1940) is a prominent French journalist and political commentator.

q.p: Sometimes hiding behind pseudonyms like Curt Vile, this English comics author wrote Watchmen, V for Vendetta, and From Hell — who is he?
q.e: Alan Moore (born 18 November 1953) is an English author known primarily for his work in comics including Watchmen, V for Vendetta, The Ballad of Halo Jones, Swamp Thing, Batman: The Killing Joke, and From Hell.

q.p: Compared to Kafka and Borges for his postmodern style, this Scottish writer illustrated his own footnote-filled books and published the era-defining 1981 novel Lanark — who is he?
q.e: Alasdair Gray (28 December 1934 - 29 December 2019) was a Scottish writer and artist.

q.p: Formerly political editor at the Daily Mirror, this strategist became Tony Blair's spokesman and speechwriter, steering Labour's rebrand as 'New Labour' before 1997 — who is he?
q.e: Alastair Campbell (born 25 May 1957) is a British journalist, author, strategist, broadcaster, and activist.

q.p: Born to pied-noir parents in French Algeria, he studied philosophy in Algiers before writing The Myth of Sisyphus and The Fall — which Nobel-winning writer?
q.e: Albert Camus (kam-OO; 7 November 1913 - 4 January 1960) was a French philosopher, novelist, author, dramatist, journalist, world federalist, and political activist.

q.p: A theologian, organist, philosopher, and physician all at once, this Alsatian polymath won the 1952 Nobel Peace Prize for his philosophy of 'Reverence for Life' — who was he?
q.e: Albert Schweitzer (14 January 1875 - 4 September 1965) was a German polymath from Alsace.

q.p: A friend of Hitler who designed the Reich Chancellery, this architect became Nazi Germany's armaments minister and served 20 years after Nuremberg — who was he?
q.e: Albert Speer (19 March 1905 - 1 September 1981) was a German architect who served as Minister of Armaments and War Production in Nazi Germany during most of World War II.

q.p: This Chilean-French avant-garde filmmaker, known for surreal cult classics, started out as a mime before founding his own theater troupe in 1947 — who is he?
q.e: Alejandro Jodorowsky (born 17 February 1929) is a Chilean and French avant-garde filmmaker.

q.p: Awarded the 1970 Nobel Prize in Literature, this Russian author exposed the Soviet Gulag system in a work that sold tens of millions of copies — who was he?
q.e: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (11 December 1918 - 3 August 2008) was a Soviet and Russian author and dissident who helped to raise global awareness of political repression in the Soviet Union, especially the Gulag prison system.

q.p: This Italian novelist's masterpiece I promessi sposi helped stabilize the modern Italian language itself — who is he?
q.e: Alessandro Manzoni (7 March 1785 - 22 May 1873) was an Italian philosopher, poet, playwright, and novelist.

q.p: This journalist wrote a memoir titled 'FutureFace,' about family mystery and belonging, and became a contributing editor at The Atlantic in 2016 — who is she?
q.e: Alex Wagner (born November 27, 1977) is an American journalist and television host.

q.p: Living from 1880 to 1921, which poet is considered the foremost lyrical voice of Russia's Silver Age?
q.e: Alexander Blok was Russian poet (1880–1921).

q.p: Which British-naturalised Russian defector and former FSB officer coined the phrase 'mafia state' and became a prominent critic of Vladimir Putin?
q.e: Alexander Litvinenko (30 August 1962 - 23 November 2006) was a British-naturalised Russian defector and former officer of the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) who specialised in tackling organised crime.

q.p: Discovered by editor Isabella Blow after his MA graduate show, this British couturier led Givenchy from 1996 to 2001 before helming his own eponymous label — who is he?
q.e: Alexander McQueen (17 March 1969 - 11 February 2010) was a British fashion designer and couturier.

q.p: This Russian-Ukrainian film director and former State Duma member has become an outspoken critic of the war in Ukraine — who is he?
q.e: Alexander Nevzorov (born on 3 August 1958) is a Russian and Ukrainian television journalist, film director and a former member of the Russian State Duma.

q.p: Born in 1973, this American visual artist based in Los Angeles examines language and written texts through painting, drawing, sculpture, video, and other media. Who is she?
q.e: Alexandra Grant (born April 4, 1973) is an American visual artist who examines language and written texts through painting, drawing, sculpture, video, and other media.

q.p: Poet Laureate through much of Victoria's reign, this English poet won Cambridge's Chancellor's Gold Medal in 1829 for a piece titled 'Timbuktu' — who was he?
q.e: Alfred, Lord Tennyson (6 August 1809 - 6 October 1892) was an English poet.

q.p: Author of The Likeability Trap and host of the Latina to Latina podcast, this television anchor previously worked at PBS's Amanpour & Company and HuffPost Live — who is she?
q.e: Alicia Menendez (-; born July 2, 1983) is an American television commentator, host, and writer.

q.p: Founder of the Party of Democratic Action, which Bosnian leader served as head of his country's presidency throughout the Bosnian War?
q.e: Alija Izetbegović (8 August 1925 - 19 October 2003) was a Bosnian politician, Islamic philosopher and author who served as the president of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1990 to 1996.

q.p: This 2014 war novel follows a blind French girl who takes refuge in Saint-Malo after the Nazi invasion, and a German boy skilled in radio technology — what book is this?
o: All the Light We Cannot See
q.e: All the Light We Cannot See is a 2014 war novel by American author Anthony Doerr.

q.p: This Beat poet, who befriended Burroughs and Kerouac at Columbia, wrote a work so incendiary that San Francisco police and US Customs seized copies of it. Who is he?
q.e: Allen Ginsberg (June 3, 1926 - April 5, 1997) was an American poet and writer.

q.p: Now a professor of international law at Oxford, this human rights barrister once defended WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange. Who is she?
q.e: Amal Clooney (ne Alamuddin; born (1978-02-03)3 February 1978) is a Lebanese and British international human rights lawyer.

q.p: This Italian painter who moved to Paris in 1906 is known for portraits with surreally elongated faces and necks — work scorned in his lifetime but later coveted; who was he?
q.e: Amedeo Modigliani (12 July 1884 - 24 January 1920) was an Italian painter and sculptor of the cole de Paris who worked mainly in France.

q.p: She helped found the Ninety-Nines, a group for female pilots, and wrote best-selling books about flying before her 1937 disappearance over the Pacific — who is she?
q.e: Amelia Earhart (born July 24, 1897; disappeared July 2, 1937; declared dead January 5, 1939) was an American aviator and aviation pioneer who became one of the most celebrated figures of early flight.

q.p: Published in 2001 by British author Neil Gaiman, this fantasy novel blends Americana with ancient and modern mythology, centered on a taciturn drifter named Shadow — name the book?
o: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
q.e: American Gods (2001) is a fantasy novel by British author Neil Gaiman. The novel is a blend of Americana, fantasy, and various strands of ancient and modern mythology, all centering on the mysterious and taciturn Shadow.

q.p: Before presenting BBC Radio 4's 'Today' programme, this journalist served as media editor for BBC News and edited a national UK newspaper — who is he?
q.e: Amol Rajan (-MOHL; born 4 July 1983) is an Indian-British journalist, broadcaster and writer working in the United Kingdom.

q.p: Before joining ABC News, this broadcaster worked at NBC News and co-hosted the Saturday edition of Today — who is she?
q.e: Amy Robach (born February 6, 1973) is an American television reporter formerly for ABC News.

q.p: This American actress and comedian played Jerri Blank on Strangers with Candy and voiced Princess Carolyn on the Netflix series BoJack Horseman — who is she?
q.e: Amy Sedaris (born March 29, 1961) is an American actress, comedian, and writer.

q.p: Active as a journalist, screenwriter, and TV host in Italy, this multi-hyphenate also dabbled in acting during a career that ended with his death in 2023 — who is he?
q.e: Andrea Purgatori (1 February 1953 - 19 July 2023) was an Italian journalist, writer, screenwriter, television presenter and occasional actor.

q.p: Called 'France's greatest contemporary man of letters' in his New York Times obituary, this Nobel laureate wrote more than fifty books — who was he?
q.e: André Gide (22 November 1869 - 19 February 1951) was a French author whose writing spanned a wide variety of styles and topics.

q.p: Owned by Rovio, a subsidiary of Sega, this puzzle-game franchise pits a flightless, anthropomorphic flock against egg-stealing rotund pigs — what's the series called?
q.e: Angry Birds is a video game series and media franchise created by Finnish game designer Jaakko Iisalo and owned by Rovio Entertainment, a subsidiary of Sega.

q.p: Leo Tolstoy called this 1878 work his first 'true' novel, yet grew to hate it while grinding out the final serialized installments — which book is it?
q.e: Anna Karenina is a novel, first published in book form in 1878, by the Russian author Leo Tolstoy.

q.p: Formerly married to a media titan whose company she also served as a director of, this British-Australian journalist and novelist passed away in February 2026 — who is she?
q.e: Anna dePeyster (ne Torv; formerly Murdoch and Mann; 30 June 1944 - 17 February 2026) was a British and Australian journalist and novelist.

q.p: Born in New Orleans and raised Catholic before turning agnostic, she launched a Gothic empire in 1976 with the book that became Interview with the Vampire — which author?
q.e: Anne Rice (born Howard Allen Frances O'Brien; October 4, 1941 - December 11, 2021) was an American author of Gothic fiction, erotic literature, and Bible fiction.

q.p: Five hours before John Lennon's murder, she took a Polaroid of him curled around Yoko Ono that became one of Rolling Stone's most famous covers — which portrait photographer?
q.e: Annie Leibovitz (born October 2, 1949) is an American portrait photographer best known for her portraits, particularly of celebrities, which often feature subjects in intimate settings and poses.

q.p: At 18, this German artist toured Van Gogh's haunts in the Netherlands, Belgium and France before building a career of straw-and-lead canvases confronting Nazi history — who is he?
q.e: Anselm Kiefer (born 8 March 1945) is a German painter and sculptor.

q.p: This 6th-century Arabian knight and poet inspired an epic romance about his adventurous life and composed one of the famed 'hanging odes' -- who is he?
q.e: Antarah ibn Shaddad (525-608 AD), also known as Antar, was a pre-Islamic Arab poet and knight belonging to the Arab tribe of Banu Abs, famous for both his poetry and his adventurous life.

q.p: Which publishing term refers to a themed collection of literary pieces — perhaps short stories, poems, or songs — gathered by a compiler rather than written by one author?
q.e: Anthology is a collection of literary works chosen by the compiler.

q.p: An English writer and composer who also lectured in phonetics and translated Cyrano de Bergerac, he's best remembered for the dystopian satire A Clockwork Orange — who was he?
q.e: Anthony Burgess (25 February 1917 - 22 November 1993) was an English writer and composer.

q.p: This Catalan architect, born in 1852, is the greatest exponent of Catalan Modernisme and created the Sagrada Família church — who is he?
q.e: Antoni Gaudí (25 June 1852 - 10 June 1926) was a Catalan architect and designer from Spain, widely known as the greatest exponent of Catalan Modernisme.

q.p: First appearing as a computer programmer in a 1984 Mirage comic, this character became a news reporter in the debut animated series and a vigilante's love interest — who is she?
q.e: April O'Neil is a fictional character from the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles comics.

q.p: This ancient Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) founded the Peripatetic school and wrote widely on natural sciences, philosophy, economics, politics, and the arts. Who is he?
q.e: Aristotle (Ancient; 384-322 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath. Shortly after Plato died, Aristotle left Athens and, at the request of Philip II of Macedon, tutored his son Alexander the Great beginning in 343 BC.

q.p: This central hero of the Hindu epic Mahabharata, the third of five Pandava brothers and a son of the king of the gods, is celebrated for his unmatched skill in archery — who is he?
q.e: Arjuna is one of the central characters of the ancient Hindu epic Mahabharata.

q.p: Winner of a Pulitzer Prize for a play about a struggling traveling salesman, this American playwright also wrote 'The Crucible' and the screenplay for 'The Misfits' — who is he?
q.e: Arthur Miller (October 17, 1915 - February 10, 2005) was an American playwright and essayist in the 20th-century American theater.

q.p: This French poet abandoned his schooling as a teenager to flee to Paris during the Franco-Prussian War, then stopped writing literature entirely by age twenty — who is he?
q.e: Arthur Rimbaud (20 October 1854 - 10 November 1891) was a French poet known for his transgressive and surreal themes and for his influence on modern literature and arts, prefiguring surrealism.

q.p: A member of the Royal Spanish Academy since 2003, this novelist spent two decades as a war correspondent before writing the Captain Alatriste adventures — who is he?
q.e: Arturo Pérez-Reverte (born 25 November 1951) is a Spanish novelist and journalist.

q.p: Ayn Rand called this 1957 doorstopper her magnum opus and the seedbed of her philosophy of Objectivism, blending science fiction, mystery, and romance — what's the novel?
q.e: Atlas Shrugged is a 1957 novel by Ayn Rand. It is her longest novel, the fourth and final one published during her lifetime, and the one she considered her magnum opus in the realm of fiction writing.

q.p: This French philosopher formulated the doctrine of positivism and coined the term 'sociology,' treating the new discipline as the crowning achievement of the sciences — who is he?
q.e: Auguste Comte (19 January 1798 - 5 September 1857) was a French philosopher, mathematician and writer who formulated the doctrine of positivism.

q.p: First introduced in H.P. Lovecraft's novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, this being tops the genealogy chart of the Cthulhu Mythos as ruler of the Outer Gods — who is he?
q.e: Azathoth is a deity in the Cthulhu Mythos and Dream Cycle stories of writer H. P. Lovecraft.

q.p: This yonkoma manga got three bonus chapters in 2009 to mark its tenth anniversary, having originally run from 1999 to 2002 in a monthly magazine - which series?
q.e: Azumanga Daioh is a Japanese yonkoma comedy manga series written and illustrated by Kiyohiko Azuma.

q.p: Born in Andijan in the Fergana Valley (now Uzbekistan) in 1483, this founder of the Mughal Empire was a descendant of both Timur and Genghis Khan. Who was he?
q.e: Babur (14 February 1483 - 26 December 1530; born Zahr ud-Dn Muhammad) was the founder of the Mughal Empire in the Indian subcontinent.

q.p: Written in the third person and published in 2007, this Lee Child novel is the eleventh in the Jack Reacher series and lent its name from an Albert King song — which title?
o: The 100: A Ranking of the Most Influential Persons in History
q.e: Bad Luck and Trouble is the eleventh book in the Jack Reacher series written by Lee Child.

q.p: Serialized from 1985 to 1994 in a Japanese girls' comics magazine, this manga by Akimi Yoshida follows street gang leader Ash Lynx through 1980s New York City — name the series?
q.e: Banana Fish (stylized in all caps) is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Akimi Yoshida.

q.p: Author of The Poisonwood Bible and the locavore memoir Animal, Vegetable, Miracle, which novelist won the 2023 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for Demon Copperhead?
q.e: Barbara Kingsolver (born April 8, 1955) is an American novelist, essayist, and poet.

q.p: This Western artistic style flourished from the early 1600s until the 1750s, following Renaissance art and preceding Rococo and Neoclassical styles. What period is this?
q.e: Baroque is a Western style of architecture, music, dance, painting, sculpture, poetry, and other arts that flourished from the early 1600s until the 1750s.

q.p: Debuting in Detective Comics #27 in 1939, this DC superhero is secretly a wealthy Gotham City philanthropist who vows never to kill his enemies — who is he?
q.e: Batman is a superhero who appears in American comic books published by DC Comics.

q.p: This sadistic Death Eater began as an unnamed background character in 'Goblet of Fire' before becoming a central antagonist in the series — who is she?
q.e: Bellatrix Lestrange is a fictional character in the Harry Potter novels by J. K. Rowling.

q.p: A two-time NCAA champion and multiple Dan Hodge Trophy winner in college wrestling, this fighter went on to reign as ONE FC's longest-serving welterweight champion — who is he?
q.e: Ben Askren (born July 18, 1984) is an American professional mixed martial artist, professional boxer and Olympic wrestler.

q.p: Author of a nonfiction account of Waterloo as well as the long-running Sharpe novels, this English writer's Saxon Stories became The Last Kingdom on TV — who is he?
q.e: Bernard Cornwell (born 23 February 1944) is an English author of historical novels and a history of the Waterloo campaign.

q.p: Set in a medieval European-style dark fantasy world, this manga follows the swordsman Guts on a quest for revenge against his former friend Griffith — name the series?
q.e: Berserk (manga) is a Japanese manga series created by Kentaro Miura.

q.p: After a shark attack cost her a left arm in 2003, this American surfer returned to professional competition and wrote about it in an autobiography — who is she?
q.e: Bethany Hamilton (born February 8, 1990) is an American professional surfer and writer.

q.p: First appearing as a Spider-Man adversary in 1979 before becoming his on-off love interest, this Marvel character is secretly cat burglar Felicia Hardy — who is she?
q.e: Black Cat (Marvel Comics) is a character appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics.

q.p: In a world where nearly everyone is born with magical ability, this manga follows a boy with no powers of his own who is granted a rare, mysterious grimoire — name the series?
q.e: Black Clover is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Yki Tabata.

q.p: Kazimir Malevich called this 1915 canvas, showing just one shape on a plain background, his breakthrough into a new art movement — which painting?
q.e: Black Square is a 1915 oil on linen canvas painting by the Russian avant-garde artist and theorist Kazimir Malevich.

q.p: Debuting as an Iron Man villain in 1964 before reforming into an Avenger two years later, this Marvel spy character got her own solo series in 1999 — who is she?
q.e: Black Widow (Natasha Romanova) is a superhero appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics.

q.p: First appearing in a 1973 Dracula comic, this half-vampire Marvel antihero was born in Soho after his mother was attacked by a vampire during childbirth — who is he?
q.e: Blade (character) is an antihero appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics.

q.p: Played by Leighton Meester, this snobbish-yet-sensitive New York socialite ruled Manhattan's social scene while a blogger tracked her every move — who is she?
q.e: Blair Waldorf (married name Bass) is one of the main characters of Gossip Girl, introduced in the original series of novels and also appearing as the lead in the television adaptation; she also appears in the comic adaptation.

q.p: This Oxfordshire country house, seat of the Dukes of Marlborough, is the birthplace of Winston Churchill and one of England's largest homes, built in the early 1700s — name it?
q.e: Blenheim Palace is a country house in Woodstock, Oxfordshire, England. Originally called Blenheim Castle, it has been known as Blenheim Palace since the 19th century.

q.p: Shot with a Mamiya RZ67 camera near the Napa–Sonoma county line, this vineyard hillside picture was bought by Microsoft in 2000 to promote Windows XP — what is it known as?
o: The Vulture and the Little Girl
q.e: Bliss (photograph) is the default wallpaper of Microsoft's Windows XP operating system.

q.p: Created by Keith Giffen, John Rogers, and Cully Hamner, this DC superhero debuted in Infinite Crisis #3 in 2006 as the third character to take up his heroic identity — who is he?
q.e: Blue Beetle (Jaime Reyes) is a superhero appearing in American comic books published by DC Comics.

q.p: At just 14 he won the first of a record eight US Championships, and in one tournament posted the only perfect 11–0 score in its history — which American chess prodigy?
q.e: Bobby Fischer (March 9, 1943 - January 17, 2008) was an American chess grandmaster and the eleventh World Chess Champion.

q.p: Before serving as UK Prime Minister, this Eton and Oxford man edited The Spectator and spent two terms as mayor of London — who is he?
q.e: Boris Johnson (born 19 June 1964) is a British politician and writer who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and Leader of the Conservative Party from 2019 to 2022.

q.p: At just 21, this novelist published the controversial bestseller Less Than Zero, later scandalizing critics with a satirical tale of a Wall Street killer — who is he?
q.e: Bret Easton Ellis (born March 7, 1964) is an American author and screenwriter.

q.p: This American actress played Laurie Keller on the sitcom Cougar Town, winning a Critics' Choice Award, after earlier roles on Freaks and Geeks and Dawson's Creek — who is she?
q.e: Busy Philipps (born June 25, 1979) is an American actress, singer and comedian.

q.p: This Berlin-based professor and Catholic theologian, born in 1959, became a leading critic of neoliberal culture — who is he?
q.e: Byung-Chul Han (born 1959) is a South Korean-born German philosopher, Catholic theologian and cultural theorist.

q.p: Launching his eponymous fashion company in 1968, this American designer went on to lend his name to a wide range of perfumes, watches, and jewelry — who is he?
q.e: Calvin Klein (born November 19, 1942) is an American fashion designer.

q.p: This Impressionist painter adopted the Neo-Impressionist style at age 54 while working alongside Georges Seurat and Paul Signac — who is he?
q.e: Camille Pissarro (piss-AR-oh; 10 July 1830 - 13 November 1903) was a Danish-French Impressionist and Neo-Impressionist painter born on the island of Saint Thomas (now in the US Virgin Islands, but then in the Danish West Indies).

q.p: In this 1759 satire by Voltaire, a sheltered young man is slowly disillusioned after being raised on his mentor's relentless philosophical optimism — what work is it?
o: The Fall of the House of Usher
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
q.e: Candide (kon-DEED or kahn-DEED) is a French satire written by Voltaire, a philosopher of the Age of Enlightenment, first published in 1759.

q.p: Long attributed to Etruscan craftsmen, this bronze depicting Romulus and Remus nursing from a wild animal was later radiocarbon-dated to the medieval period — which sculpture?
q.e: Capitoline Wolf is a bronze sculpture depicting a scene from the legend of the founding of Rome.

q.p: Missing a hand since Peter Pan fed it to a crocodile, this Jolly Roger-commanding pirate dreads the sight of blood — who is he?
q.e: Captain Hook is the main antagonist of J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan stories.

q.p: Debuting in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas, this Jules Verne character is driven by a hatred of imperialism as he commands his submarine, the Nautilus — who is he?
q.e: Captain Nemo (also known as Prince Dakkar) is a character created by the French novelist Jules Verne (1828-1905).

q.p: Serialized in Weekly Shōnen Jump, this Japanese manga follows a boy chasing his dream in the sport of football, through friendships, rivalries, and match after match — what is it?
q.e: Captain Tsubasa is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Yichi Takahashi.

q.p: A Catalan politician born in 1962 who became president of Catalonia in 2016, held an independence referendum, and served as an MEP from 2019 to 2024. Who is he?
q.e: Carles Puigdemont (Catalan; born 29 December 1962) is a Catalan politician and journalist from Spain.

q.p: This Uruguayan entrepreneur and former rugby player, the son of a well-known painter, was one of only 16 survivors of a 1972 plane crash in the Andes mountains — who is he?
q.e: Carlos Páez Rodríguez (born October 31, 1953) is a Uruguayan entrepreneur and former rugby player.

q.p: This Spanish novelist's 2001 book about a shadow and the wind sold 15 million copies and made a 2007 list of the best Spanish-language books of the previous 25 years — who is he?
q.e: Carlos Ruiz Zafón (Spanish; 25 September 1964 - 19 June 2020) was a Spanish novelist known for his 2001 novel La sombra del viento (The Shadow of the Wind).

q.p: Published serially from 1871 to 1872, this novella's title vampire is considered literature's prototype for female and lesbian vampire characters — which work?
q.e: Carmilla is an 1872 Gothic novella by Irish author Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu.

q.p: The only surviving child of a US president and his First Lady, this author and attorney went on to serve as her country's ambassador to both Japan and Australia — who is she?
q.e: Caroline Kennedy (born November 27, 1957) is an American author, diplomat, and attorney.

q.p: This 1963 novel was Kurt Vonnegut's fourth, blending science fiction with dark satire about the purpose of religion — which book?
o: The Fall of the House of Usher
q.e: Cat's Cradle is a satirical postmodern novel, with science fiction elements, by American writer Kurt Vonnegut.

q.p: Founder of a South Los Angeles rehab complex for aggressive dogs, this television personality's show has aired in more than 80 countries since 2004 — who is he?
q.e: Cesar Millan (mil-AHN,; born August 27, 1969) is a Mexican-American dog trainer.

q.p: In this manga, a poor teenager named Denji fuses with a dog-like devil to gain the power to transform parts of his body into blades — name the series?
q.e: Chainsaw Man is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Tatsuki Fujimoto.

q.p: This French poet's most famous collection of lyric poetry captures the changing nature of beauty amid Baron Haussmann's sweeping renovation of 19th-century Paris — who is he?
q.e: Charles Baudelaire (9 April 1821 - 31 August 1867) was a French poet, essayist, translator and art critic.

q.p: A competitive dancer for over a decade before going viral in late 2019, this TikTok personality became the platform's most-followed creator from 2020 to 2022 — who is she?
q.e: Charli D'Amelio (d-; born May 1, 2004) is an American social media personality and dancer.

q.p: Created by Charles M. Schulz, which perpetually nervous, self-doubting 'lovable loser' is the principal character of the comic strip Peanuts?
q.e: Charlie Brown is the principal character of the American comic strip Peanuts, created by Charles M. Schulz. Depicted as a "lovable loser", Charlie Brown is a popular and widely recognized cartoon character.

q.p: To save a pig named Wilbur from slaughter, a barn spider spins words like "Some Pig" and "Radiant" into her web — naming which beloved 1952 children's book by E. B. White?
q.e: Charlotte's Web is a book of children's literature by American author E. B. White.

q.p: Which American author turned her solitary 1995 Pacific Crest Trail hike into a bestselling memoir made into a 2014 Oscar-nominated film?
q.e: Cheryl Strayed (ne Nyland; born September 17, 1968) is an American writer and podcast host.

q.p: This Italian influencer built her following via a blog called The Blonde Salad before a 2021 charity-fraud scandal engulfed her public image — who is she?
q.e: Chiara Ferragni (born 7 May 1987) is an Italian blogger and influencer.

q.p: Often called Arthur C. Clarke's finest work, this 1953 novel imagines Earth's benevolent conquest by enigmatic alien Overlords at the cost of human culture — which book?
o: The Fall of the House of Usher
q.e: Childhood's End is a 1953 science fiction novel by the British author Arthur C. Clarke.

q.p: This American model made her professional debut in the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue in 2010 and later co-hosted the musical competition show Lip Sync Battle. Who is she?
q.e: Chrissy Teigen (born November 30, 1985) is an American model, television personality, and author.

q.p: This British-Iranian journalist serves as CNN's Chief International Anchor and also co-hosts a talk show with her ex-husband, former U.S. official James Rubin — who is she?
q.e: Christiane Amanpour (born 12 January 1958) is a British-Iranian journalist and television host.

q.p: Serialized in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1985 to 1991, this manga by Tsukasa Hojo spawned an anime adaptation and a wider media franchise across multiple countries — what is it?
q.e: City Hunter is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Tsukasa Hojo.

q.p: Born in 1840, this French painter founded Impressionism and is seen as a key precursor to modernism through his plein air landscape paintings. Who is he?
q.e: Claude Monet (14 November 1840 - 5 December 1926) was a French painter and founder of Impressionism who is seen as a key precursor to modernism, especially in his attempts to paint nature as he perceived it.

q.p: This English broadcaster co-presented Strictly Come Dancing for over a decade and won a BAFTA in 2023 for hosting the reality series The Traitors — who is she?
q.e: Claudia Winkleman (born 15 January 1972) is an English broadcaster and writer.

q.p: This British author burst onto the horror scene in the 1980s with his Books of Blood, then wrote and directed the first film in a chilling series — who is he?
q.e: Clive Barker (born 5 October 1952) is a British writer, filmmaker, and visual artist.

q.p: At 92 cm long, this is the largest surviving medieval illuminated manuscript, nicknamed the 'Devil's Bible' for its full-page portrait of Satan — what is it?
o: The 100: A Ranking of the Most Influential Persons in History
q.e: Codex Gigas ("Giant Book") is the largest extant medieval illuminated manuscript in the world, at a length of 92 cm (36 in).

q.p: This musical dramatizes how a Newfoundland town housed thousands of diverted airline passengers in the days following the September 11 attacks — which show?
o: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child
q.e: Come from Away is a 2017 musical, with book, music and lyrics by Irene Sankoff and David Hein.

q.p: This visual medium combines sequential panels of images with text devices like speech balloons and onomatopoeia to convey narrative — what is it called?
q.e: Comics is a medium used to express ideas with images, often combined with text or other visual information.

q.p: This German-born broadcaster, born in June 1979, reports for TV stations in both German and Arabic — who is he?
q.e: Constantin Schreiber (born 14 June 1979) is a German journalist working for German and Arabic language TV stations.

q.p: Played by Donald Sutherland as the dictator of a dystopian nation, this Hunger Games character is reimagined as a scheming teenage mentor in a 2020 prequel novel — who is he?
q.e: Coriolanus Snow is a character in The Hunger Games franchise, a book series and film series.

q.p: Dostoevsky's first great novel after a decade of Siberian exile, it traces the tormented Rodion Raskolnikov through the streets of Saint Petersburg — what is it?
q.e: Crime and Punishment is a novel by the Russian author Fyodor Dostoevsky.

q.p: Ranging from a quick disapproving remark to a detailed written response, this practice comes in theoretical, practical, and impressionistic forms — what's it called?
q.e: Criticism is the construction of a judgement about the negative or positive qualities of someone or something.

q.p: In this 1781 book, Immanuel Kant sets out to determine the limits and scope of metaphysics by examining the human mind's own capacity for rational thought. Name the book?
q.e: Critique of Pure Reason (1781; second edition 1787) is a book by the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, in which the author seeks to determine the limits and scope of metaphysics.

q.p: This Parisian avant-garde movement rejected the single viewpoint, breaking subjects apart and showing them from multiple angles at once — what is it called?
q.e: Cubism is an early-20th-century avant-garde art movement which began in Paris.

q.p: Created by Margret and H.A. Rey, which beloved storybook monkey debuted as a character named 'Fifi' in a 1939 French-published book?
q.e: Curious George is a fictional monkey who is the title character of a series of popular children's picture books written and illustrated by Margret and H. A. Rey.

q.p: A libertine author of the early 1600s, his science-fiction novels about lunar and solar voyages were published only after his death in 1655 — who was he?
q.e: Cyrano de Bergerac (d, - BAIR-,; 6 March 1619 - 28 July 1655) was a French novelist, playwright, epistolarian, and duelist.

q.p: This Japanese manga set in an alternate 19th century follows a young exorcist who fights a demonic army called Akuma using an ancient substance called Innocence — what is it?
q.e: D.Gray-man is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Katsura Hoshino.

q.p: Born into poverty on a Missouri farm, this self-improvement author and teacher wrote the enduring bestseller 'How to Win Friends and Influence People' in 1936 — who is he?
q.e: Dale Carnegie (spelled Carnagey until c.

q.p: Blacklisted as one of the Hollywood Ten, this screenwriter behind Spartacus and Exodus kept working clandestinely, winning hidden Oscars under other names — who was he?
q.e: Dalton Trumbo (December 9, 1905 - September 10, 1976) was an American screenwriter who scripted many award-winning films, including Thirty Seconds Over Tokyo (1944), Roman Holiday (1953), Spartacus (1960), and Exodus (1960).

q.p: Created by Grant Morrison and Andy Kubert, this character is Batman's youngest child, with adopted siblings including Dick Grayson and Jason Todd — who is he?
q.e: Damian Wayne (n al Ghul) is a superhero appearing in American comic books published by DC Comics, commonly in association with Batman.

q.p: Compelled to love the vampire Katherine Pierce a century earlier, this character returns to Mystic Falls and falls for a mortal look-alike named Elena Gilbert — who is he?
q.e: Damon Salvatore is a fictional character in L. J. Smith's novel series The Vampire Diaries.

q.p: Created by Jack Kirby and formerly known as Uxas, this DC Comics tyrant rules the planet Apokolips and seeks the Anti-Life Equation to enslave the multiverse — who is he?
q.e: Darkseid is a supervillain appearing in American comic books published by DC Comics.

q.p: Styling himself as a self-proclaimed English gangster, this real-life figure later reinvented himself as both an author and an actor — who was he?
q.e: Dave Courtney (17 February 1959 - 22 October 2023) was an English self-proclaimed gangster who became both an author and an actor.

q.p: Carved by Michelangelo between 1501 and 1504, this 17-foot marble figure was the first colossal statue since antiquity and was meant for a cathedral roofline — what is it?
q.e: David (Michelangelo) is a masterpiece of Italian Renaissance sculpture in marble created from 1501 to 1504 by Michelangelo.

q.p: Known for raw, frenetic figurative paintings he calls 'dirty style,' this Los Angeles artist has also illustrated for magazines like Hustler and Vice — who is he?
q.e: David Choe (born April 22, 1976) is an American artist, actor, journalist, and podcast host from Los Angeles.

q.p: Nicknamed a 'workhorse reporter' by Slate, this New Yorker writer authored a book about obsession in the Amazon that hit No. 1 on the bestseller list — who is he?
q.e: David Grann (born March 10, 1967) is an American journalist, a staff writer for The New Yorker, and author.

q.p: This English WWII author was branded by a British court in 2000, after a failed libel case, for falsely claiming Hitler didn't know of the extermination of Jews — who is he?
q.e: David Irving (born 24 March 1938) is an English author who has written on the military and political history of the Second World War, especially Nazi Germany.

q.p: This Japanese manga, written by Ryohgo Narita and serialized in Square Enix's Young Gangan since 2017, was adapted into a two-cour anime that aired throughout 2023. What is it?
q.e: Dead Mount Death Play is a Japanese manga series written by Ryohgo Narita and illustrated by Shinta Fujimoto.

q.p: This Tony-winning musical follows a socially anxious high school senior who invents an outsized role for himself in the aftermath of a classmate's tragedy — what show is it?
o: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child
q.e: Dear Evan Hansen is a stage musical with music and lyrics by Benj Pasek and Justin Paul, and a book by Steven Levenson.

q.p: A finalist for the 2017 Hugo Award, this novel follows The Three-Body Problem and The Dark Forest to complete Liu Cixin's trilogy — which book is this?
o: The Fall of the House of Usher
q.e: Death's End is a science fiction novel by the Chinese writer Liu Cixin.

q.p: This 2022 Barbara Kingsolver novel reimagines 'David Copperfield' in contemporary Appalachia and swept the Pulitzer and Women's Prize for Fiction — which book?
q.e: Demon Copperhead is a 2022 novel by Barbara Kingsolver. It was a co-recipient of the 2023 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, and won the 2023 Women's Prize for Fiction.

q.p: Once at the center of a 1998 lobbying scandal, this English psychotherapist later became known for enduring one of the most severe long COVID cases on record — who is he?
q.e: Derek Draper (15 August 1967 - 3 January 2024) was an English political lobbyist and psychotherapist.

q.p: This literary and theatrical form depicting an exchange between two or more people traces its Western roots to the Socratic method of Plato — what is it?
q.e: Dialogue (sometimes spelled dialog in American English) is an interactive communication between two or more people, and a literary and theatrical form that depicts such an exchange.

q.p: Besides hosting public radio's The Savvy Traveler and competing on Dancing with the Stars, she's famous for marathon ocean swims — who is this athlete and author?
q.e: Diana Nyad (ne Sneed; born August 22, 1949) is an American author, journalist, motivational speaker, and long-distance swimmer.

q.p: This Australian professional dancer joined a British ballroom competition in 2017 and picked up a BAFTA in 2025 after finally winning the contest the year before. Who is she?
q.e: Dianne Buswell (born 6 May 1989) is an Australian professional dancer who is best known for her appearances on the British television show Strictly Come Dancing.

q.p: Once always handwritten and now often kept online, this dated day-by-day personal record can also serve institutional purposes like government or military logs — what is it called?
q.e: Diary is a written or audiovisual memorable record, with discrete entries arranged by date reporting on what has happened over the course of a day or other period.

q.p: Composed by Johann Strauss II to a libretto by Karl Haffner and Richard Genée, this comic operetta premiered in 1874 — which work?
o: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child
q.e: Die Fledermaus is an operetta composed by Johann Strauss II to a German libretto by Karl Haffner and Richard Gene, which premiered in 1874.

q.p: This is the second opera performed in Wagner's Ring cycle, even though he wrote its libretto third — which opera is it?
o: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child
q.e: Die Walküre (German; The Valkyrie), WWV 86B, is the second of the four epic music dramas that constitute Richard Wagner's cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen.

q.p: This German Lutheran pastor helped found the anti-Nazi Confessing Church and wrote a 1937 book on Christian discipleship still considered a modern classic today — who was he?
q.e: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (4 February 1906 - 9 April 1945) was a German Lutheran pastor, neo-orthodox theologian and anti-Nazi dissident who was a key founding member of the Confessing Church.

q.p: A former journalist for Euronews and RT, this author now lives outside Russia after his Metro 2033 novels made him internationally famous — who is he?
q.e: Dmitry Glukhovsky is a Russian and Israeli author, best known for the science fiction novel Metro 2033 and its sequels.

q.p: Once a member of the Kyiv City Council, this Ukrainian broadcaster runs two YouTube channels that each earned a Gold Creator Award for topping a million subscribers — who is he?
q.e: Dmitry Gordon (Dmytro Illich Hordon,; born 21 October 1967) is a Ukrainian journalist, TV host, and blogger.

q.p: This Ministry of Magic appointee's refusal to teach practical Dark Arts defense at Hogwarts pushed the students to secretly form their own defense club — who is she?
q.e: Dolores Umbridge is a fictional character from the Harry Potter series created by J. K. Rowling.

q.p: This 28-volume shōnen manga by Kei Sasuga ran in Weekly Shōnen Magazine from 2014 to 2020 and got a 2019 TV anime from Diomedéa airing on MBS's Animeism block — which series?
q.e: Domestic Girlfriend is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Kei Sasuga.

q.p: This American sculptor moved from small tabletop pieces to massive free-standing bronze works in the 1980s, and has long been married to actress Meryl Streep — who is he?
q.e: Don Gummer (born December 12, 1946) is an American sculptor.

q.p: She chaired Chicago State University's English department and is best remembered as the mother of rapper Kanye — who is she?
q.e: Donda West (ne Williams; July 12, 1949 - November 10, 2007) was an American educator and chair of Chicago State University's Department of English, Communications, Media, and Theater.

q.p: Time named her one of its 100 Most Influential People in 2014, the same year a film adaptation of her Pulitzer-winning 2013 novel appeared — which American novelist?
q.e: Donna Tartt (born December 23, 1963) is an American novelist.

q.p: This manga stars an earless robotic cat who travels back in time from the 22nd century to help a young boy named Nobita in his daily life — name the character?
q.e: Doraemon is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Fujiko F. Fujio.

q.p: Born to British parents in Iran and raised in Southern Rhodesia, this novelist behind The Golden Notebook won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2007 — who is she?
q.e: Doris Lessing (ne Tayler; 22 October 1919 - 17 November 2013) was a British novelist - sometimes identified as Rhodesian early in her career - and winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2007.

q.p: In this Japanese manga by Q Hayashida, an amnesiac man with a reptile's head teams up with his friend to recover his memories in a violent, magic-warped world — what series is it?
q.e: Dorohedoro is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Q Hayashida.

q.p: This British political commentator and Spectator associate editor wrote a controversial 2017 book warning about immigration, identity, and Islam in Europe. Who is he?
q.e: Douglas Murray (author) (born 16 July 1979) is a British conservative political commentator, cultural critic, author, and journalist.

q.p: Inducted into the Poker Hall of Fame after a 60-year career, this player won the WSOP Main Event twice, back-to-back in 1976 and 1977 — who is he?
q.e: Doyle Brunson (August 10, 1933 - May 14, 2023) was an American poker player who played professionally for over 60 years.

q.p: Dropping out of Oxford in 1927 to draw for Vanity Fair and Life, this American went on to write 60-plus wildly popular children's books under a doctorly pen name — what name?
q.e: Dr. Seuss (sooss, zoyss -; March 2, 1904 - September 24, 1991) was an American children's author, illustrator, animator, and cartoonist.

q.p: Bram Stoker filled over a hundred pages of notes drawing on folklore for this 1897 horror novel, in which Abraham Van Helsing leads a group hunting a vampire count — what is it?
o: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
q.e: Dracula is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker.

q.p: Serialized from 2004 to 2014 in Weekly Morning, which manga follows two rival oenophiles hunting down twelve legendary vintages nicknamed the 'Apostles'?
o: More Than a Married Couple, But Not Lovers
q.e: Drops of God is a Japanese manga series about wine.

q.p: This American columnist wrote Elle magazine's advice column for over two decades, then filed civil lawsuits accusing Donald Trump of sexual assault — who is she?
q.e: E. Jean Carroll (born December 12, 1943) is an American journalist, author, and advice columnist.

q.p: Nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature 22 separate times, this Edwardian-era English novelist co-wrote the libretto for Britten's opera Billy Budd — who is he?
q.e: E. M. Forster (1 January 1879 - 7 June 1970) was an English author.

q.p: Considered by its Nobel Prize-winning author to be his magnum opus, this 1952 family saga novel was originally addressed to the writer's own young sons. Name the novel?
q.e: East of Eden (novel) is a 1952 family saga novel by American author and Nobel Prize winner John Steinbeck.

q.p: Once a cold-hearted miser who despised the holiday season, this Dickens character is transformed by a night of ghostly visitations in an 1843 novella — who is he?
q.e: Ebenezer Scrooge is a fictional character and the protagonist of Charles Dickens's 1843 novella A Christmas Carol.

q.p: Inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame, this American author of "The House of Mirth" and "Ethan Frome" was born Newbold Jones in 1862 — who is she?
q.e: Edith Wharton (ne Jones; January 24, 1862 - August 11, 1937) was an American writer and designer.

q.p: A childhood shadowed by illness and a family mental condition fed the anguished 'soul painting' of which Norwegian, creator of one of Western art's most iconic 1893 images?
q.e: Edvard Munch (MUUNK; 12 December 1863 - 23 January 1944) was a Norwegian painter.

q.p: Mentored by Gustav Klimt, this Austrian Expressionist filled canvases with twisted bodies, raw sexuality, and many nude self-portraits before dying in 1918 at just 28. Who is he?
q.e: Egon Schiele (12 June 1890 - 31 October 1918) was an Austrian Expressionist painter.

q.p: Born July 18, 1969, this American journalist and author wrote a memoir that sold over 12 million copies and was made into a film in 2010 — who is she?
q.e: Elizabeth Gilbert (born July 18, 1969) is an American journalist and author. The book was also made into a film of the same name in 2010.

q.p: Named by Smithsonian among the "100 Most Significant Americans of All Time," this 19th-century author and church co-founder reportedly received over 2,000 visions — who was she?
q.e: Ellen G. White (ne Harmon; November 26, 1827 - July 16, 1915) was an American author, and was both the prophet and a co-founder of the Seventh-day Adventist Church.

q.p: Son of Eärendil and Elwing, this Tolkien character served as herald to an Elf-king and later ruled a hidden elven refuge for thousands of years — who is he?
q.e: Elrond is a fictional character in J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth legendarium.

q.p: This legal analyst co-hosts Fox News's daytime talk show Outnumbered and frequently appears on The Five and Gutfeld! — who is she?
q.e: Emily Compagno (born November 9, 1979) is a legal analyst and American television host who co-hosts the daytime news and talk show Outnumbered on Fox News.

q.p: Largely unpublished during her lifetime yet now regarded as canonical, this American poet from Amherst, Massachusetts wrote in a distinctively elliptical style — who is she?
q.e: Emily Dickinson (December 10, 1830 - May 15, 1886) was an American poet.

q.p: This Jane Austen comedy of manners, set in the fictional Surrey village of Highbury, examines the concerns of genteel young women in Georgian-Regency England — what novel is it?
q.e: Emma (novel) is a novel written by English author Jane Austen.

q.p: This Russian-born revolutionary drew crowds of thousands to her lectures on anarchist philosophy and women's rights after immigrating to the US in 1885 — who is she?
q.e: Emma Goldman (June 27, 1869 - May 14, 1940) was a Russian-born anarchist revolutionary, political activist, and writer.

q.p: Born November 26, 1994, this Canadian works as both a dancer and a choreographer — who is she?
q.e: Emma Portner (born November 26, 1994) is a Canadian professional dancer and choreographer.

q.p: Born on 9 December 1957, which French author, screenwriter, and film director works across all three of those crafts?
q.e: Emmanuel Carrère (born 9 December 1957) is a French author, screenwriter and film director.

q.p: Published continuously in English since 1768 and finally going online-only in 2016, this reference work's last print edition ran to 32 volumes — what is it?
o: The 100: A Ranking of the Most Influential Persons in History
q.e: Encyclopædia Britannica (Latin for 'British Encyclopdia') is a general-knowledge English-language encyclopaedia.

q.p: Raised in Oak Park, Illinois, this 1954 Nobel laureate wrote in a famously spare, understated style and was romanticized for his adventurous, blunt public image — who was he?
q.e: Ernest Hemingway (July 21, 1899 - July 2, 1961) was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist.

q.p: Drawing on Hippocrates of Chios and Eudoxus of Cnidus, this deductive mathematical treatise is often called the most successful textbook ever written — which ancient work?
o: The 100: A Ranking of the Most Influential Persons in History
q.e: Euclid's Elements (Ancient) is a mathematical treatise written c. 300 BC by the Ancient Greek mathematician Euclid.

q.p: This novel in verse by Alexander Pushkin, published serially from 1825 to 1832, gave Russian literature its archetype of the brooding 'superfluous man' — what work is it?
q.e: Eugene Onegin is a novel in verse written by Alexander Pushkin. The first complete edition was published in 1833, and the currently accepted version is based on the 1837 publication.

q.p: Serialized for over seven years in Futabasha's Manga Action before ending in December 2024, this manga also became a spring 2023 live-action drama — which series?
o: Even If You Don't Do It
Firefighter! Daigo of Fire Company M
q.e: Even If You Don't Do It (Anata ga Shite Kurenakutemo) is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Haru Haruno.

q.p: Born in Saint Paul and famous for novels of 1920s excess, this American writer popularized the term "Jazz Age" yet earned real acclaim only after his death — who is he?
q.e: F. Scott Fitzgerald (September 24, 1896 - December 21, 1940), widely known as F. Scott Fitzgerald, was an American novelist.

q.p: A practicing lawyer before turning to fiction in his mid-forties, which German author's books have sold millions of copies in over 35 languages?
q.e: Ferdinand von Schirach (born 12 May 1964) is a German lawyer and writer.

q.p: Portrayed by Austin Butler in Dune: Part Two, which treacherous nephew and heir of Baron Vladimir Harkonnen was first played on screen by Sting in 1984?
q.e: Feyd-Rautha is a fictional character in the 1965 science fiction novel Dune by Frank Herbert.

q.p: Originally self-published as an ebook in 2011, this erotic romance novel follows a college graduate's deepening BDSM relationship with a young business magnate — what is it?
q.e: Fifty Shades of Grey is a 2011 erotic romance novel by British author E. L. James.

q.p: Serialized for years as 'Work in Progress,' this Joyce novel writes English warped with words from many languages to mimic a half-dreaming mind — what's its final title?
o: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman
q.e: Finnegans Wake is a novel by the Irish writer James Joyce.

q.p: Published in 2018 and later adapted into HBO's House of the Dragon, this George R. R. Martin book traces the centuries-long reign of House Targaryen — which book?
o: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time
q.e: Fire & Blood (novel) is a fantasy book by American writer George R. R. Martin.

q.p: Drawn originally by Alex Raymond, this comic-strip hero debuted in 1934 as a space-faring rival to Buck Rogers — who is he?
q.e: Flash Gordon is the protagonist of a space adventure comic strip created and originally drawn by Alex Raymond.

q.p: A statistician as well as a healer, this founder of modern nursing organized care for the wounded at Constantinople during the Crimean War. Who was she?
q.e: Florence Nightingale (12 May 1820 - 13 August 1910) was an English social reformer, statistician and the founder of modern nursing.

q.p: In this 1979 Gothic novel, four siblings are locked away in a house under the tyrannical control of their mother and grandmother, narrated by the eldest sister — what book is it?
o: The 100: A Ranking of the Most Influential Persons in History
q.e: Flowers in the Attic is a 1979 Gothic novel by V. C. Andrews.

q.p: The largest of the eusocial wasps, some species in this genus can exceed 50 millimetres in length. What insect is it?
q.e: For Whom the Bell Tolls is a novel by Ernest Hemingway published in 1940.

q.p: An iconoclastic feminist poet who also directed film, she shook up Iranian literature before dying in a car crash at 32 — who is she?
q.e: Forugh Farrokhzad (29 December 1934 - 14 February 1967) was an influential Iranian poet and film director.

q.p: First published by Gnome Press in 1951, this Isaac Asimov novel wove together five interrelated short stories to launch what became a sprawling series — name the book?
q.e: Foundation (Asimov novel) is a science fiction novel by American writer Isaac Asimov.

q.p: Known for sardonic social commentary steeped in New York City sensibilities, this author and cultural critic ran with the 1970s-80s art scene crowd around Andy Warhol — who is she?
q.e: Fran Lebowitz (born October 27, 1950) is an American author, public speaker, cultural critic, and actor.

q.p: He argued that real knowledge comes only from inductive reasoning and careful observation of nature, all while serving as Attorney General under James I — which philosopher?
q.e: Francis Bacon (22 January 1561 - 9 April 1626) was an English philosopher and statesman who served as Attorney General and Lord Chancellor of England under King James I.

q.p: This Irish-born British painter built raw, unsettling triptychs around a single motif — screaming popes, crucifixions, figures trapped in geometric cages — who was he?
q.e: Francis Bacon (artist) (28 October 1909 - 28 April 1992) was an Irish-born British figurative painter known for his raw, unsettling imagery.

q.p: Blending film noir with manga influences, this graphic novelist gave the world Sin City, 300, and a groundbreaking take on Batman in The Dark Knight Returns — who is he?
q.e: Frank Miller (born January 27, 1957) is an American comic book creator, screenwriter, and director known for his comic book stories and graphic novels.

q.p: Nicknamed 'Lefty,' this sports-betting expert and Las Vegas casino boss was the real-life inspiration for the character Sam 'Ace' Rothstein in Casino — who was he?
q.e: Frank Rosenthal (June 12, 1929 - October 13, 2008) was an American professional sports gambler, Las Vegas casino executive, organized crime associate, and FBI informant.

q.p: Subtitled 'The Modern Prometheus,' this 1818 Gothic novel tells of a young scientist who builds a living creature from assorted body parts — what is its main title?
q.e: Frankenstein is an 1818 Gothic novel written by English author Mary Shelley.

q.p: A German-language Jewish writer from Prague whose isolated heroes battle incomprehensible bureaucracies — his name became an adjective. Who is it?
q.e: Franz Kafka (3 July 1883 - 3 June 1924) was a German-language Jewish Czech writer and novelist born in Prague, in the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

q.p: Serialized from 2006 to 2010, this manga pits twelve holders of prophetic notebooks against each other in a lethal game for the throne of the universe — which series?
q.e: Future Diary is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Sakae Esuno.

q.p: Born in what is now Ukraine, this Russian survivalist and marine explorer also became an Eastern Orthodox priest in December 2010 — who is he?
q.e: Fyodor Konyukhov (born 12 December 1951 in Chkalovo, Pryazovskyi Raion, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukrainian SSR) is a Russian survivalist, voyager and marine explorer.

q.p: This paradox-loving English Christian apologist dreamed up a humble priest-detective named Father Brown and converted from Anglicanism to Catholicism — who is he?
q.e: G. K. Chesterton (29 May 1874 - 14 June 1936) was an English Christian apologist writer.

q.p: Affectionately called 'Gabo' across Latin America, this Colombian writer left law school for journalism and went on to win the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature — who is he?
q.e: Gabriel García Márquez (Latin American; 6 March 1927 - 17 April 2014) was a Colombian writer and journalist, known affectionately as Gabo or Gabito throughout Latin America.

q.p: An exorcist for the Diocese of Rome, this Pauline priest became a famous and controversial figure for his work in demonology, claiming tens of thousands of exorcisms — who was he?
q.e: Gabriele Amorth (1 May 1925 - 16 September 2016) was an Italian Catholic priest of the Paulines and an exorcist for the Diocese of Rome.

q.p: Once a mortal man, this cosmic Marvel entity now devours entire planets to sustain his life force — who is he?
q.e: Galactus is a fictional character appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics.

q.p: First appearing in a 1975 issue of Strange Tales, this superhuman combatant was portrayed on screen by Zoe Saldaña — who is she?
q.e: Gamora is a character appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics.

q.p: This Azerbaijani politician held a seat in her country's National Assembly for nearly two decades, from 2005 to 2023 — who is she?
q.e: Ganira Pashayeva was an Azerbaijani politician who was a Member of the National Assembly of Azerbaijan from 2005 until her death in 2023.

q.p: In this Japanese manga, two men who died in a train accident are recruited into a deadly afterlife 'game' hunting aliens with futuristic weapons — what's the Hiroya Oku series?
q.e: Gantz (stylized in all caps) is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Hiroya Oku.

q.p: This reclusive sorcerer, accompanied by his cat Azrael, is the perennial antagonist of a Belgian cartoonist's blue-skinned creations, always scheming to capture them — who is he?
q.e: Gargamel is a fictional character and the main antagonist of The Smurfs media franchise created by Belgian cartoonist Peyo.

q.p: Composed over centuries starting in the first millennium CE, this Hindu scripture devotes thousands of verses to topics from heaven and hell to ancestral rites — which text?
o: Do not go gentle into that good night
q.e: Garuda Purana is one of 18 Mahapuranas in Hinduism.

q.p: Fill in the blank: “____ (born 17 July 1970) is a Canadian writer, podcaster, far-right commentator and founder of the Proud Boys.”
q.e: Gavin McInnes (born 17 July 1970) is a Canadian writer, podcaster, far-right commentator and founder of the Proud Boys. During his time at Vice, McInnes was called a leading figure in the New York hipster subculture.

q.p: Co-host of CBS Mornings and an editor-at-large for Oprah Daily, she was named one of Time's 100 Most Influential People in 2019 — who is she?
q.e: Gayle King (born December 28, 1954) is an American television personality, author and broadcast journalist for CBS News, co-hosting its flagship morning program, CBS Mornings, and before that its predecessor CBS This Morning.

q.p: Living across the bridge from Enlightenment to Romanticism, this German idealist read the Napoleonic wars through a philosophical lens — who is he?
q.e: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (27 August 1770 - 14 November 1831) was a German philosopher and a major figure in the tradition of German idealism.

q.p: At age 79, this cigar-smoking comedian won an Academy Award for The Sunshine Boys, decades after teaming with his wife on radio and TV — who is he?
q.e: George Burns (born Nathan Birnbaum; January 20, 1896 - March 9, 1996) was an American comedian, actor, writer, and singer, and one of the few entertainers whose career successfully spanned vaudeville, radio, film, and television.

q.p: Before becoming an ABC News anchor, this former Democratic advisor served as White House communications director in the 1990s — who is he?
q.e: George Stephanopoulos (born February 10, 1961) is an American television host, political commentator, and former Democratic advisor.

q.p: This French singer-songwriter turned poems by Louis Aragon and other celebrated writers into elegant songs for voice and guitar — who is he?
q.e: Georges Brassens was a French singer-songwriter and poet. Georges Charles Brassens (French: [ʒɔʁʒ(ə) ʃaʁl bʁasɛ̃s]; Occitan: [ˈbɾasens]) was a French singer-songwriter and poet.

q.p: Combining a mathematical precision of mind with painstaking dots of color, this artist devised chromoluminarism and kickstarted Neo-Impressionism — who is he?
q.e: Georges Seurat (2 December 1859 - 29 March 1891) was a French post-Impressionist artist.

q.p: Born in Liège and later living in France, the US, and Switzerland, this prolific Belgian writer also penned literary works he called 'romans durs' — who is he?
q.e: Georges Simenon (12/13 February 1903 - 4 September 1989) was a Belgian writer who created the fictional detective Jules Maigret.

q.p: Adapted into a 2017 film by Mike Flanagan, this Stephen King suspense novel traps its heroine handcuffed to a bed after her husband's fatal heart attack — what's the novel?
o: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a Fuck
q.e: Gerald's Game is a 1992 suspense novel by American writer Stephen King.

q.p: Working across abstract painting, photorealism, and glass, this German visual artist born in 1932 has been called the greatest living painter — who is he?
q.e: Gerhard Richter (born 9 February 1932) is a German visual artist.

q.p: This American writer made her Paris salon a hub for Picasso and Hemingway, then penned a memoir of those years entirely in the voice of her partner, Alice B. Toklas — who is she?
q.e: Gertrude Stein (February 3, 1874 - July 27, 1946) was an American novelist, poet, playwright, and art collector.

q.p: She's the only daughter among Arthur and Molly's children in J.K. Rowling's wizarding saga, and ends up marrying the boy who lived — who is she?
q.e: Ginny Weasley is a fictional character in the Harry Potter series of novels by J. K. Rowling.

q.p: Compared to Badal Sarkar in Bengali and Vijay Tendulkar in Marathi, which 1960s playwright marked the coming of age of modern Kannada theatre and later won the Jnanpith Award?
q.e: Girish Karnad (19 May 1938 - 10 June 2019) was an Indian playwright, actor, film director, Kannada writer, and a Jnanpith awardee, who predominantly worked in Kannada, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Marathi films.

q.p: Housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague since 1902, this Vermeer oil painting from around 1665 — known in Dutch as Meisje met de parel — has inspired novels and films. What is it?
q.e: Girl with a Pearl Earring is an oil painting by Dutch Golden Age painter Johannes Vermeer, dated c.

q.p: A former First Amendment lawyer turned blogger, this journalist began publishing explosive national-security reports at The Guardian in June 2013 — who is he?
q.e: Glenn Greenwald (born March 6, 1967) is an American journalist, author, and former lawyer.

q.p: Born Hannah in 1895, this British painter created an iconic self-portrait with lover Nesta Obermer and refused to be addressed by any gendered title — who is this artist?
q.e: Gluck (painter) (born Hannah Gluckstein; 13 August 1895 - 10 January 1978) was a British painter.

q.p: A notable figure in the Risorgimento, this Italian poet and patriot wrote the lyrics to what would become his country's national anthem. Who was he?
q.e: Goffredo Mameli (Italian; 5 September 1827 - 6 July 1849) was an Italian patriot, poet and writer who was a notable figure in the Risorgimento.

q.p: Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel follows Scarlett O'Hara clawing out of poverty after Sherman's March to the Sea — its title comes from an Ernest Dowson poem. What is it?
q.e: Gone with the Wind (novel) is a novel by American writer Margaret Mitchell, first published in 1936.

q.p: Sharing an author with the Acts of the Apostles and together accounting for over a quarter of the New Testament, this is the third of the four canonical Gospels — which one?
q.e: Gospel of Luke is the third of the New Testament's canonical Gospels. It tells of the origins, birth, ministry, death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus.

q.p: Written by an author who himself fled Nigeria during the Biafran War, this 2004 novel follows a teenager named Elvis navigating corruption and poverty in Lagos — which novel?
q.e: GraceLand is a 2004 novel by Chris Abani, which tells the story of a teenager named Elvis, who is trying to get out of the ghettos of Lagos, Nigeria.

q.p: A restaurant critic for The Guardian and a regular judge on BBC's 'MasterChef', this British writer has also authored eleven novels for teenagers. Who is she?
q.e: Grace Dent (born 3 October 1973) is a British columnist, broadcaster and author.

q.e: Pierre Curie is a physicist. Pierre Curie (15 May 1859 – 19 April 1906) was a French physicist and chemist, and a pioneer in crystallography and magnetism.

q.p: Who among these is a mathematician?
q.e: Leonhard Euler is a mathematician. Euler has been called a "universal genius" who "was fully equipped with almost unlimited powers of imagination, intellectual gifts and extraordinary memory".

q.p: Pick the mathematician from these four.
q.e: Jim Simons is a mathematician. James Harris Simons (April 25, 1938 – May 10, 2024) was an American hedge fund manager, investor, mathematician, and philanthropist.

q.e: Ted Kaczynski is a mathematician. The FBI used the case identifier UNABOM (University and Airline Bombing) before his identity was known, resulting in the media naming him the "Unabomber".

q.p: Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
q.e: Omar Khayyam is a mathematician. Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.

q.p: Which of these four is a mathematician?
q.e: Isaac Newton is a mathematician. Newton contributed to and refined the scientific method, and his work is considered the most influential in bringing forth modern science.

q.p: Pick the chemist from these four.
q.e: Primo Levi is a chemist. Primo Michele Levi (Italian: [ˈpriːmo ˈlɛːvi]; 31 July 1919 – 11 April 1987) was a Jewish Italian chemist, partisan, Holocaust survivor and writer.

q.p: Who among these is a chemist?
q.e: Dmitri Mendeleev is a chemist. The synthetic element mendelevium is named in his honor.

q.p: What is the atomic number of Zirconium?
q.e: Zirconium is a chemical element; it has symbol Zr and atomic number 40.

q.p: In what year was Michael Rockefeller born?
q.e: Michael Rockefeller: Michael Clark Rockefeller (May 18, 1938; disappeared November 19, 1961) was an American anthropologist and art collector and member of the Rockefeller family.

q.p: In what year was Émile Durkheim born?
q.e: Émile Durkheim: David Émile Durkheim (French: [emil dyʁkɛm] or [dyʁkajm]; 15 April 1858 – 15 November 1917) was a French sociologist.

q.e: Max Born: During World War I, Born was originally placed as a radio operator, but his specialist knowledge led to his being moved to research duties on sound ranging.

q.p: In what year was Ursula von der Leyen born?
q.e: Ursula von der Leyen: Von der Leyen was born and raised in Brussels, Belgium, to German parents.

q.p: In what year was Ümit Özdağ born?
q.e: Ümit Özdağ: On 16 November 2020, Özdağ was also dismissed from the Good Party.

q.p: In what year did Michael Rockefeller die?
