q.e: Michael Rockefeller: Michael Clark Rockefeller (May 18, 1938; disappeared November 19, 1961) was an American anthropologist and art collector and member of the Rockefeller family.

q.p: In what year did Émile Durkheim die?
q.e: Émile Durkheim: David Émile Durkheim (French: [emil dyʁkɛm] or [dyʁkajm]; 15 April 1858 – 15 November 1917) was a French sociologist.

q.p: In what year was Molybdenum discovered?
q.e: Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.

q.p: In what year was Special relativity discovered?
q.e: Special relativity: In physics, the special theory of relativity, or simply special relativity, is a scientific theory of the relationship between space and time.

q.p: In what year was HIV/AIDS discovered?
q.e: HIV/AIDS: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a retrovirus that attacks the immune system.

q.p: In what year was Factitious disorder imposed on another discovered?
q.e: Factitious disorder imposed on another: The victim is typically the caregiver's child but is occasionally an adult partner.

q.p: In what year was Citric acid discovered?
q.e: Citric acid is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7.

q.p: In what year was Coriolis force discovered?
q.e: Coriolis force: In physics, the Coriolis force is a pseudo-force that acts on objects in motion within a frame of reference that rotates with respect to an inertial frame.

q.p: In what year was Bayes' theorem discovered?
q.e: Bayes' theorem: The theorem was developed in the 18th century by Bayes and independently by Pierre-Simon Laplace.

q.p: In what year was Euler's formula discovered?
q.e: Euler's formula: The formula is still valid if x is a complex number, and is also called Euler's formula in this more general case.

q.p: In what year was Huntington's disease discovered?
q.e: Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea, is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that is usually inherited.

q.p: In what year was Klinefelter syndrome discovered?
q.e: Klinefelter syndrome (KS), also known as 47,XXY, is a chromosome anomaly.

q.p: In what year was Möbius strip discovered?
q.e: Möbius strip: In mathematics, a Möbius strip, Möbius band, or Möbius loop is a surface that can be formed by attaching the ends of a strip of paper together with a half-twist.

q.p: In what year was Mass–energy equivalence discovered?
q.e: Mass–energy equivalence: In physics, mass–energy equivalence is the relationship between mass and energy in a system's rest frame.

q.p: In what year was Theobroma cacao discovered?
q.e: Theobroma cacao (cacao tree or cocoa tree) is a small (6–12 m (20–39 ft) tall) evergreen tree in the Malvaceae family.

q.p: In what year was Uncertainty principle discovered?
q.e: Uncertainty principle: The uncertainty principle, also known as Heisenberg's indeterminacy principle, is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics.

q.p: In what year was Adenosine triphosphate discovered?
q.e: Adenosine triphosphate: When consumed in a metabolic process, ATP converts either to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) or to adenosine monophosphate (AMP).

q.p: In what year was Mustard gas discovered?
q.e: Mustard gas: There is no preventive agent against mustard gas, with protection depending entirely on skin and airways protection, and no antidote exists for mustard poisoning.

q.p: In what year was Coulomb's law discovered?
q.e: Coulomb's law: This electric force is conventionally called the electrostatic force or Coulomb force.

q.p: Who founded Genetics?
q.e: Genetics: Gregor Mendel. Genetics is the study of genes, genetic variation, and heredity in organisms.

q.p: Who created COBOL?
q.e: COBOL: CODASYL. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.

q.p: Who created Information theory?
q.e: Information theory: Claude Shannon. Information theory is the mathematical study of the quantification, storage, and communication of a particular type of mathematically defined information.

q.p: Who created Bash (Unix shell)?
q.e: Bash (Unix shell): Brian Fox. Bash (short for "Bourne Again SHell") is an interactive command interpreter and command language developed for Unix-like operating systems.

q.p: Which company manufactures Harrier jump jet?
q.e: Harrier jump jet: Hawker Siddeley. The Harrier emerged as the only truly successful V/STOL design of the many attempted during that era.

q.p: Which company manufactures Mikoyan MiG-29?
q.e: Mikoyan MiG-29: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The Mikoyan MiG-29 (Russian: Микоян МиГ-29; NATO reporting name: Fulcrum) is a twin-engine fighter aircraft designed in the Soviet Union.

q.p: Which company manufactures Potassium chloride?
q.e: Potassium chloride: Pfizer. Potassium chloride (KCl, or potassium salt) is a metal halide salt composed of potassium and chlorine.

q.p: Which company manufactures Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet?
q.e: Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet: McDonnell Douglas. The Super Hornet is in service with the armed forces of the United States, Australia, and Kuwait.

q.p: Which company manufactures Magnesium sulfate?
q.e: Magnesium sulfate: Pfizer. It is a white crystalline solid, soluble in water.

q.p: Which company manufactures Sodium acetate?
q.e: Sodium acetate: Pfizer. Sodium acetate is a chemical compound with formula CH3COONa, also abbreviated NaOAc.

q.p: Which company manufactures Prunus domestica?
q.e: Prunus domestica: People's Republic of China. Prunus domestica is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae.

q.p: Which company manufactures CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder?
q.e: CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder: Chengdu Aircraft Industry Group. The JF-17 can be used for multiple roles, including interception, ground attack, anti-ship, and aerial reconnaissance.

q.p: Which country is General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon from?
q.e: General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon: United States. The aircraft was first developed by General Dynamics in 1974.

q.p: Which country is Dassault Falcon 900 from?
q.e: Dassault Falcon 900: France. The Dassault Falcon 900, commonly abbreviated as the F900, is a French-built corporate trijet aircraft made by Dassault Aviation.

q.p: In which country is Harrier jump jet?
q.e: Harrier jump jet: United Kingdom. The Harrier emerged as the only truly successful V/STOL design of the many attempted during that era.

q.p: In which country is Royal Society?
q.e: Royal Society: United Kingdom. Founded on 28 November 1660, it was granted a royal charter by King Charles II and is the oldest continuously existing scientific academy in the world.

q.p: In which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21 based?
q.e: Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21: Soviet Union. Approximately 60 countries across four continents have flown the MiG-21, and it still serves many nations seven decades after its maiden flight.

q.p: In which country is Embraer E-Jet E2 family based?
q.e: Embraer E-Jet E2 family: Brazil. The Embraer E-Jet E2 family is a series of four-abreast narrow-body regional jet airliners designed and produced by the Brazilian aircraft manufacturer Embraer.

q.p: Which country is Boeing 777X from?
q.e: Boeing 777X: United States. The Boeing 777X is an American long-range, wide-body, twin-engine airliner built by Boeing Commercial Airplanes, undergoing flight testing.

q.p: In which country did the Hawker Hurricane take place?
q.e: Hawker Hurricane: United Kingdom. The Air Ministry ordered Hawker's Interceptor Monoplane in late 1934, and the prototype Hurricane K5083 performed its maiden flight on 6 November 1935.

q.p: In which country is Dassault Mirage 2000?
q.e: Dassault Mirage 2000: France. Work on what would become the Mirage 2000 originated with the "Delta 1000" project launched in 1972.

q.p: In which country is Fish and chips?
q.e: Fish and chips: United Kingdom. Fish and chips is a hot dish consisting of battered and fried fish, served with chips.

q.p: In which country is Virgo interferometer?
q.e: Virgo interferometer: Italy. The Virgo interferometer is a large-scale scientific instrument near Pisa, Italy, for detecting gravitational waves.

q.p: In which country did the Junkers Ju 87 take place?
q.e: Junkers Ju 87: Germany. The Junkers Ju 87, popularly known as the "Stuka", is a German dive bomber and ground-attack aircraft.

q.p: In which country is Blood orange?
q.e: Blood orange: Italy. The blood orange is a variety of orange with crimson, near blood-colored flesh.

q.p: In which country is Minamata disease?
q.e: Minamata disease: Japan. Minamata disease (Japanese: 水俣病, Hepburn: Minamata-byō) is a neurological disease caused by severe mercury poisoning.

q.p: In which country is Māori language?
q.e: Māori language: New Zealand. The southernmost member of the Austronesian language family, it is related to Cook Islands Māori, Tuamotuan, and Tahitian.

q.p: In which country is Gaboon viper?
q.e: Gaboon viper: Gabon. It is the largest member of the genus Bitis.

q.p: Which country is Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil from?
q.e: Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil: France. The AS355 Ecureuil 2 is a twin-engine variant, marketed in North America as the TwinStar.

q.p: In which country is Kazan phenomenon?
q.e: Kazan phenomenon: Soviet Union. The Kazan mafia was known to be particularly cruel in their extortion tactics, and periodically brought in reinforcements from Tatarstan.

q.p: Which country is Bombardier Challenger 600 series from?
q.e: Bombardier Challenger 600 series: Canada. At the end of 1975, Canadair began funding the development of LearStar 600, and then bought the design for a wide-cabin business jet in April 1976.

q.p: In which country did the CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder take place?
q.e: CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder: People's Republic of China. The JF-17 can be used for multiple roles, including interception, ground attack, anti-ship, and aerial reconnaissance.

q.p: In which country is Thalidomide scandal?
q.e: Thalidomide scandal: Germany. It was introduced as a sedative and medication for morning sickness without having been tested on pregnant women.

q.p: Which country is Yakovlev MC-21 based from?
q.e: Yakovlev MC-21: Russia. The aircraft made its maiden flight on 28 May 2017 from Irkutsk.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Archaeopteryx?
q.e: Archaeopteryx: Carl Friedrich Häberlein. Archaeopteryx (lit. 'ancient wing'), sometimes referred to by its German name, "Urvogel " (lit. 'Primeval Bird') is an extinct genus of bird-like dinosaurs.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Gaussian integral?
q.e: Gaussian integral: Leonhard Euler. The integral has a wide range of applications.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering General relativity?
q.e: General relativity: Albert Einstein. The relation is specified by the Einstein field equations, a system of second-order partial differential equations.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Graph theory?
q.e: Graph theory: Leonhard Euler. In mathematics and computer science, graph theory is the study of graphs, which are mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Newton's law of universal gravitation?
q.e: Newton's law of universal gravitation: Robert Hooke. This is a general physical law derived from empirical observations by what Isaac Newton called inductive reasoning.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Factitious disorder imposed on another?
q.e: Factitious disorder imposed on another: Roy Meadow. The victim is typically the caregiver's child but is occasionally an adult partner.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Citric acid?
q.e: Citric acid: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Citric acid is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Spontaneous generation?
q.e: Spontaneous generation: Anaximander. It was hypothesized that certain forms, such as fleas, could arise from inanimate matter such as dust, or that maggots could arise from dead flesh.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Reynolds number?
q.e: Reynolds number: Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet. At low Reynolds numbers, flows tend to be dominated by laminar (sheet-like) flow, while at high Reynolds numbers, flows tend to be turbulent.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Hubble's law?
q.e: Hubble's law: Georges Lemaître. The Friedmann equations showed the universe might be expanding, and presented the expansion speed if that were the case.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Cauchy–Schwarz inequality?
q.e: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: Viktor Bunyakovsky. It is considered one of the most important and widely used inequalities in mathematics.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering L'Hôpital's rule?
q.e: L'Hôpital's rule: Johann Bernoulli. The differentiation of the numerator and denominator often simplifies the quotient or converts it to a limit that can be directly evaluated by continuity.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Cherenkov radiation?
q.e: Cherenkov radiation: Sergey Vavilov. A classic example of Cherenkov radiation is the characteristic blue glow of an underwater nuclear reactor.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Carbon dioxide?
q.e: Carbon dioxide: Jan Baptist van Helmont. Carbon dioxide is a chemical compound with the chemical formula CO2.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering 2C-B?
q.e: 2C-B: Alexander Shulgin. 2C-B, also known as 4-bromo-2,5-dimethoxyphenethylamine or by names such as Nexus or Erox, is a psychedelic drug of the phenethylamine and 2C families.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Hydrogen cyanide?
q.e: Hydrogen cyanide: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Hydrogen cyanide (also called prussic acid) is a chemical compound with the formula HCN and structural formula H−C≡N.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Allergic rhinitis?
q.e: Allergic rhinitis: John Bostock. It is classified as a type I hypersensitivity reaction.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Mass–energy equivalence?
q.e: Mass–energy equivalence: Albert Einstein. In physics, mass–energy equivalence is the relationship between mass and energy in a system's rest frame.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Silicon carbide?
q.e: Silicon carbide: Edward Goodrich Acheson. Silicon carbide (SiC), also known as carborundum, is a hard chemical compound of silicon and carbon.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Theobroma cacao?
q.e: Theobroma cacao: Christopher Columbus. Theobroma cacao (cacao tree or cocoa tree) is a small (6–12 m (20–39 ft) tall) evergreen tree in the Malvaceae family.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Uncertainty principle?
q.e: Uncertainty principle: Werner Heisenberg. The uncertainty principle, also known as Heisenberg's indeterminacy principle, is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering TON 618?
q.e: TON 618: Braulio Iriarte.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Stirling's approximation?
q.e: Stirling's approximation: Abraham de Moivre. In mathematics, Stirling's approximation (or Stirling's formula) is an asymptotic approximation for factorials.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Multiple sclerosis?
q.e: Multiple sclerosis: Jean-Martin Charcot. It is a type of demyelinating disease, where the nervous system's ability to transmit signals is damaged.

q.p: Who is credited with discovering Influenza A virus?
q.e: Influenza A virus: Christopher Andrewes. Influenza A virus, or IAV, is a pathogen with strains that cause seasonal flu in humans; it can also infect birds and some mammals.

q.p: Russell Crowe stars in this 2001 Ron Howard film about a Nobel Prize-winning mathematician's struggle with schizophrenia, based on Sylvia Nasar's biography. What's the title?
q.e: A Beautiful Mind (film) is a 2001 American biographical drama film about the mathematician John Nash who won a Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

q.p: Stretching from the thoracic diaphragm to the pelvic brim, this body region sits between the chest and the pelvis — which body part?
q.e: Abdomen (also belly or stomach in vertebrates, or metasoma in arthropods) is the front part of the torso between the thorax (chest) and pelvis in humans and in other vertebrates.

q.p: This Onmyōdō master advised Heian emperors on astrology and spiritual matters; a Kyoto shrine and an Osaka train station now honor him — who is he?
q.e: Abe no Seimei (February 21, 921 AD - October 31, 1005) was a Japanese onmyji, a court official and specialist of Onmyd, during the middle of the Heian period.

q.p: This localized collection of pus builds up within body tissue, usually from bacterial infection, causing redness, pain, warmth, and swelling. What is it?
q.e: Abscess is a collection of pus that has built up within the tissue of the body, usually caused by bacterial infection.

q.p: Found on every continent except Antarctica, this family of hook-billed raptors includes buzzards, vultures, and kites across 75 genera — which family is this?
q.e: Accipitridae is one of the four families within the order Accipitriformes, and is a family of small to large birds of prey with strongly hooked bills and variable morphology based on diet.

q.p: About 5 million tonnes of acetic acid are produced annually largely to make this compound, most commonly in polymer form — what is it?
q.e: Acetate is a salt formed by the combination of acetic acid with a base (e.g. sodium hydroxide), an ester of acetic acid, or the anion CH3COO- found in solution.

q.p: With the formula (CH3)2CO, this volatile solvent is produced by the millions of tonnes yearly, much of it to make precursors for plastics like bisphenol A — what is it?
q.e: Acetone (2-propanone or dimethyl ketone) is an organic compound with the formula (CH3)2CO.

q.p: Drugs that meddle with this neurotransmitter can do everything from paralyze to cause convulsions, since it's the signal motor neurons use to activate muscles. What is it?
q.e: Acetylcholine (ACh) is an organic compound that functions in the brain and body of many types of animals (including humans) as a neurotransmitter.

q.p: First unearthed in Montana in 1987 by a team led by Jack Horner, this horned dinosaur genus takes its name from a Greek river deity — name the genus?
q.e: Achelousaurus is a genus of centrosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous Period of what is now North America, about 77 to 74.8 million years ago.

q.p: Taken as a pill, cream, or injection, this antiviral medication is the go-to treatment for herpes simplex, chickenpox, and shingles — what is it?
q.e: Aciclovir is an antiviral medication. It is primarily used for the treatment of herpes simplex virus infections, chickenpox, and shingles.

q.p: This tall wetland monocot, also known as muskrat root, may be toxic if ingested and has no proven clinical benefit despite traditional medicinal use — which plant?
q.e: Acorus calamus (also called sweet flag, sway or muskrat root, among many other common names) is a species of flowering plant with psychoactive chemicals.

q.p: First added to the DSM in 1980 and diagnosed in women twice as often as men, this condition describes an intense, maladaptive reaction to a stressful life event — what is it?
q.e: Adjustment disorder is a mental disorder defined by a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor.

q.p: Sitting atop the kidneys, this pair of endocrine glands produces hormones including adrenaline, aldosterone, and cortisol. What organ is it?
q.e: Adrenal gland (also known as suprarenal glands) are endocrine glands that produce a variety of hormones including adrenaline and the steroids aldosterone and cortisol.

q.p: Despite the conspiracy buzz, this violet compound is mass-produced, sold to the public, and not a controlled substance — its hemostatic derivative is carbazochrome. What is it?
q.e: Adrenochrome is a chemical compound produced by the oxidation of adrenaline (epinephrine).

q.p: When a message is designed to spark an immediate purchase, it's called the 'direct-response' kind of this consumer-facing practice. What is it?
q.e: Advertising is the practice and techniques employed to bring attention to a product or service.

q.p: Often confused with the unrelated sweet chestnut, this large deciduous tree in the maple, soapberry, and lychee family bears hermaphroditic flowers — what tree is it?
q.e: Aesculus hippocastanum is a species of flowering plant in the maple, soapberry and lychee family Sapindaceae.

q.p: This tsetse-fly-borne parasitic infection, caused by a protozoan, disproportionately affects humans and cattle across Africa — what is it?
o: Atrocities in the Congo Free State
q.e: African trypanosomiasis is an insect-borne parasitic infection of humans and other animals caused by the protozoan species Trypanosoma brucei, which is transmitted by the bite of an infected tsetse fly.

q.p: Home to both edible and poisonous species, this fungal genus supplies the West's most popular cultivated mushrooms, including the everyday button mushroom — which genus is it?
q.e: Agaricus is a genus of mushroom-forming fungi containing both edible and poisonous species, with over 400 members worldwide and possibly again as many disputed or newly discovered species.

q.p: Roughly two-thirds of the 150,000 people who die each day succumb to causes linked to this gradual, damage-driven process of growing older — what is it?
q.e: Ageing (or aging in American English) is the process of becoming older.

q.p: Sometimes called ajowan caraway or carom, this annual herb in the carrot family produces a seed-like fruit often confused with lovage — what is it?
q.e: Ajwain (Trachyspermum ammi) - also known as ajowan caraway, thymol seeds, bishop's weed, or carom - is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.

q.p: Heading Switzerland's Federal Department of Home Affairs for over a decade, this politician succeeded Marija Pejčinović Burić atop a major European institution in 2024 — who is he?
q.e: Alain Berset (French; born 9 April 1972) is a Swiss politician who served as a Member of the Swiss Federal Council from 2012 to 2023.

q.p: First nominated by Ronald Reagan in 1987 and reappointed every four years until 2006, this economist ran the Federal Reserve for its second-longest tenure ever — who is he?
q.e: Alan Greenspan (born March 6, 1926) is an American economist who served as the 13th chairman of the Federal Reserve from 1987 to 2006.

q.p: These large seabirds of the tubenose order range widely across the Southern Ocean and North Pacific, but are notably absent from the North Atlantic today. What birds are they?
q.e: Albatross are large seabirds related to the procellariids, storm petrels, and diving petrels in the order Procellariiformes (the tubenoses).

q.p: This Swiss chemist discovered the structure of chitin in 1929 and decades later authored a memoir titled 'LSD: My Problem Child' — who was he?
q.e: Albert Hofmann (11 January 1906 - 29 April 2008) was a Swiss chemist known for being the first to synthesize, ingest, and learn of the psychedelic effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD).

q.p: Which diverse group of aquatic photosynthetic organisms excludes land plants but includes seaweeds that can grow up to 50 metres long?
q.e: Algae (UK also; sing.: alga) are any of a large and diverse group of photosynthetic organisms.

q.p: This English academic and broadcaster, an anatomist and archaeologist by training, was president of the charity Humanists UK from 2019 to 2022 — who is she?
q.e: Alice Roberts (born 19 May 1973) is an English academic, anatomist, archaeologist, TV presenter and author.

q.p: This exaggerated immune reaction causes the body to mistake a harmless substance for a threat, triggering symptoms from a runny nose to a full anaphylactic reaction — what is it?
q.e: Allergy is an exaggerated immune response where the body mistakenly identifies an ordinarily harmless allergen as a threat.

q.p: First approved in the United States in 1966, this xanthine oxidase inhibitor treats high uric acid levels linked to gout, kidney stones, and chemotherapy — what medication is it?
q.e: Allopurinol is a medication used to decrease high blood uric acid levels.

q.p: First described by Othniel C. Marsh in 1877, this late Jurassic theropod's name means 'different lizard,' a nod to its unusually lightweight vertebrae — what dinosaur is it?
q.e: Allosaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived 155 to 143 million years ago during the late Jurassic period (latest Oxfordian to latest Tithonian ages).

q.p: A close relative of the peach in the genus Prunus, this drupe's seed isn't a true nut and can be "blanched" by softening its skin in hot water before peeling — what is it?
q.e: Almond (Prunus amygdalus, syn.

q.p: This genus of more than 650 flowering succulent species includes a 'true' member cultivated worldwide as the standard source for a soothing pharmaceutical gel — what's the genus?
q.e: Aloe (also written Alo) is a genus containing over 650 species of flowering succulent plants.

q.p: Believed to be an autoimmune attack that breaches the immune privilege of hair follicles, this condition typically leaves a few coin-sized bald spots on the scalp — what is it?
q.e: Alopecia areata (AA), also known as spot baldness, is a condition in which hair is lost from some or all areas of the body.

q.p: A military pilot who became the first astronaut representing Turkey, he reached the International Space Station on 18 January 2024 aboard the Axiom Mission 3 flight — who is he?
q.e: Alper Gezeravcı (born 2 December 1979) is a military pilot and the first Turkish astronaut.

q.p: With one stable isotope and the rank of 12th-most-abundant element in the universe, this lightweight metal carries atomic number 13 — what is it?
q.e: Aluminium (the Commonwealth and preferred IUPAC name) or aluminum (North American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Al and atomic number 13.

q.p: This amphoteric compound forms a gelatinous precipitate in water and occurs naturally as the mineral gibbsite, one of bauxite's key components — what is it?
q.e: Aluminium hydroxide is a white chemical compound that is found as the mineral gibbsite (also known as hydrargillite) and its three much rarer polymorphs: bayerite, doyleite, and nordstrandite.

q.p: This Indian economist won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on welfare economics and has also studied the causes of famines — who is he?
q.e: Amartya Sen (born 3 November 1933) is an Indian economist and philosopher.

q.p: These tropical arachnids are nicknamed 'whip-spiders,' yet they spin no silk and carry no venom — their name actually means 'blunt tail.' Which order are they?
q.e: Amblypygi is an order of arachnids also known as whip-spiders or tailless whip-scorpions, not to be confused with whip-scorpions or vinegaroons that belong to the related order Uropygi.

q.p: This large, muscular mastiff-type dog breed descends from ancestors brought to the British North American colonies, where they worked on small farms and ranches — what's the breed?
q.e: American Bulldog is a large, muscular breed of mastiff-type dog.

q.p: Given by mouth, IV, or directly into bone marrow, which antiarrhythmic medication treats conditions like ventricular tachycardia but risks serious lung and thyroid side effects?
q.e: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic medication used to treat and prevent a number of types of cardiac dysrhythmias.

q.p: The simplest pnictogen hydride, with the formula NH3, this pungent gas is also a common nitrogenous waste in living things — what is it?
q.e: Ammonia is an inorganic chemical compound of nitrogen and hydrogen with the formula NH3.

q.p: This cation forms when a proton attaches to ammonia, giving living organisms a vital source of nitrogen — what ion is it?
q.e: Ammonium is a modified form of ammonia that has an extra hydrogen atom.

q.p: This parasitic intestinal illness, caused by Entamoeba histolytica, can produce cysts that survive for weeks in soil or nearly an hour under fingernails — what is it called?
q.e: Amoebiasis is an infection of the intestines caused by a parasitic amoeba Entamoeba histolytica.

q.p: In this group of diseases, misfolded proteins clump into fibrils and accumulate in body tissue, sometimes causing an enlarged tongue or carpal tunnel syndrome — name the condition?
q.e: Amyloidosis is a group of diseases in which abnormal proteins, known as amyloid fibrils, build up in tissue.

q.p: This group of large, semiaquatic boas native to tropical South America includes the green species, among the largest snakes on Earth — name the group?
q.e: Anaconda are a group of large boas of the genus Eunectes.

q.p: Found on every continent but Antarctica and almost always monogamous breeders, which bird family unites ducks, geese, and swans under one scientific name?
q.e: Anatidae are the biological family of water birds that includes ducks, geese, and swans.

q.p: In 1978, a run-in with a particle accelerator's proton beam left this Russian physicist with an extraordinary survival story after it passed straight through his head — who is he?
q.e: Anatoli Bugorski (born 25 June 1942) is a Russian retired particle physicist.

q.p: From a Greek word meaning 'dissection,' which old branch of natural science is paired with physiology to study living things' structure and function?
q.e: Anatomy (from Ancient Greek (anatom) 'dissection') is the branch of morphology concerned with the study of the internal and external structure of organisms and their parts.

q.p: Despite overseeing Soviet thermonuclear weapons development, this physicist won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize for his activism on human rights and individual freedom — who is he?
q.e: Andrei Sakharov (21 May 1921 - 14 December 1989) was a Soviet physicist and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, which he was awarded in 1975 for emphasizing human rights around the world.

q.p: Closely related to Hepatica and Pulsatilla, which flowering plant genus in the buttercup family is nicknamed the windflower?
q.e: Anemone is a genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae.

q.p: A balloon-like bulge at a weakened patch of vessel wall, it can turn lethal in the brain's circle of Willis or the aorta if it bursts — what is this?
q.e: Aneurysm is an outward bulging, likened to a bubble or balloon, caused by a localized, abnormal, weak spot on a blood vessel wall.

q.p: This deep-tissue swelling — of the face, tongue, throat, or limbs — comes on within minutes to hours and is driven by either histamine or bradykinin — what is it?
q.e: Angioedema is an area of swelling (edema) of the lower layer of skin and tissue just under the skin or mucous membranes.

q.p: This order of ray-finned fish is named for a modified fin ray that dangles like bait to lure in prey, much like a human with a fishing rod — what are they called?
q.e: Anglerfish are ray-finned fish in the order Lophiiformes. The majority are bottom-dwellers, being demersal fish, while the aberrant deep-sea anglerfish are pelagic, (mostly) living high in the water column.

q.p: This unit of length equals one ten-billionth of a meter, or 100 picometres, and is named after a 19th-century Swedish physicist — what is it?
q.e: Angstrom (ONG-) is a unit of length equal to 1010 m; that is, one ten-billionth of a metre, a hundred-millionth of a centimetre, 0.1 nanometre, or 100 picometres.

q.p: This psychological term describes a diverse set of deficits in the ability to feel or anticipate pleasure, and is recognized as a diagnostic feature in the DSM-5 — what's the term?
q.e: Anhedonia is a diverse array of deficits in hedonic function, including reduced motivation or ability to experience pleasure.

q.p: Multicellular, oxygen-breathing, and all descended from a single common ancestor, this kingdom ranges in size from 8.5 micrometers to 33.6 meters. What is it?
q.e: Animal are multicellular, eukaryotic organisms belonging to the biological kingdom Animalia.

q.p: Its scientific name translates roughly to 'fused lizard,' and it may be the largest of its armored kind at up to 8 tons — which dinosaur genus?
q.e: Ankylosaurus is a genus of armored dinosaur. It was named by Barnum Brown in 1908; it is monotypic, containing only A. magniventris.

q.p: This type of long-term arthritis causes inflammation where the spine meets the pelvis, with lower back pain as its hallmark symptom. What condition is it?
q.e: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis from the disease spectrum of axial spondyloarthritis.

q.p: Nicknamed the 'nail mosquito,' this genus — first classified in 1818 — is the sole mosquito genus known to carry human malaria — which genus is it?
q.e: Anopheles is a genus of mosquito first described by the German entomologist J. W. Meigen in 1818.

q.p: This symptom, not a diagnosis by itself, refers to a loss of appetite in humans and — under the name 'inappetence' — in animals from dogs to goats. Which symptom?
q.e: Anorexia (symptom) is a medical term for a loss of appetite.

q.p: These eusocial insects evolved from vespoid wasps back in the Cretaceous, and you can spot one by its elbowed antennae and pinched, node-like waist. Which creature is it?
q.e: Ant are eusocial insects of the family Formicidae and, along with the related wasps and bees, belong to the order Hymenoptera.

q.p: Nicknamed 'the heart of the scorpion,' this distinctly reddish variable star is the brightest in the constellation Scorpius — what is it?
q.e: Antares is the brightest star in the constellation of Scorpius. It has the Bayer designation α Scorpii, which is Latinised to Alpha Scorpii.

q.p: Best known for his laws of planetary motion, this German astronomer has also been called the 'father of science fiction' for his novel Somnium. Who is he?
q.e: Antelope is any of the extant or recently extinct species of the ruminant artiodactyl family Bovidae, which are indigenous to most of Africa, India, the Middle East, Central Asia, and a small area of Russia.

q.p: Whether contracted through the skin, the lungs, or the gut, this Bacillus-driven infection can take up to two months to show symptoms — what is it?
q.e: Anthrax is an infection caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis or Bacillus cereus biovar anthracis.

q.p: This scientific discipline bridges biology and sociology, studying human behavior, cultures, societies, and languages across time. What field is it?
q.e: Anthropology is the scientific study of humanity that crosses biology and sociology, concerned with human behavior, human biology, cultures, societies, and linguistics, in both the present and past, including archaic humans.

q.p: What term describes the discipline of measuring human body dimensions, applied everywhere from ergonomics and architecture to tracking historical living standards?
q.e: Anthropometry (from Ancient Greek (nthrpos) 'human' and (mtron) 'measure') refers to the measurement of the human individual.

q.p: It can't touch a virus or a fungus, but a few varieties even fight protozoa — this class of drug is the frontline weapon against bacterial infection; what is it?
q.e: Antibiotic is a type of antimicrobial substance active against bacteria.

q.p: This lustrous grey metalloid, found mainly in the mineral stibnite, was historically powdered for use as a cosmetic known by its Arabic name, kohl. What element is it?
q.e: Antimony is a chemical element with the symbol Sb (from Latin stibium) and atomic number 51.

q.p: Found only on male deer, except reindeer, this branching structure of bone and cartilage falls off and regrows from scratch each year — what is it?
q.e: Antler are extensions of an animal's skull found in members of the Cervidae (deer) family.

q.p: A physician who called medicine his lawful wife and literature his mistress, this Russian writer produced four stage classics and ranks among modernism's founders — who is he?
q.e: Anton Chekhov was Russian dramatist and author (1860–1904).

q.p: Largely self-taught, this Dutch tradesman-turned-scientist pioneered the use of the microscope and is commonly called the 'Father of Microbiology' — who is he?
q.e: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (AHN-tə-nee vahn LAY-vən-hook, -huuk; 24 October 1632 - 26 August 1723) was a Dutch microbiologist and microscopist in the Golden Age of Dutch art, science and technology.

q.p: With 1,248 built, this turboprop's design was adapted from an earlier Soviet transport aircraft and became NATO's 'Cub' — which four-engine workhorse?
q.e: Antonov An-12 (NATO reporting name: Cub) is a four-engined turboprop transport aircraft designed in the Soviet Union.

q.p: NATO codenamed 'Curl' and nicknamed 'Nastia' in the USSR, this twin-engine turboprop transport was later license-built in China as the Xi'an Y-7 — what is it?
q.e: Antonov An-26 (NATO reporting name: Curl, nicknamed Nastia in the USSR) is a twin-engined turboprop regional airliner and military transport aircraft, designed and produced in the Soviet Union from 1969 to 1986.

q.p: This Portuguese economist-turned-dictator ruled as head of government from 1932 to 1968, rebranding his authoritarian regime as the corporatist 'New State.' Who is he?
q.e: António de Oliveira Salazar (28 April 1889 - 27 July 1970) was a Portuguese dictator, academic, and economist who served as President of the Council of Ministers of Portugal from 1932 to 1968.

q.p: Fill in the blank: “____ (April 21, 1971 - September 30, 2011) was an American-Yemeni Islamic cleric and lecturer.”
q.e: Anwar al-Awlaki (April 21, 1971 - September 30, 2011) was an American-Yemeni Islamic cleric and lecturer. Al-Awlaki was the first U.S. citizen to be targeted and assassinated by a U.S. government drone strike.

q.p: This emotion is defined by dread over events that haven't happened yet, distinguishing it from fear, which responds to a threat that's already present. What is it?
q.e: Anxiety is an emotion characterized by an unpleasant state of inner turmoil and includes feelings of dread over anticipated events.

q.p: Most often caused by stroke or head trauma, which condition impairs a person's ability to comprehend or formulate language because specific brain regions aren't working?
q.e: Aphasia is an impairment in a person's ability to comprehend or formulate language because of dysfunction in specific brain regions.

q.p: The 16th-largest family of flowering plants, this aromatic group includes cumin, fennel, and coriander alongside deadly relatives like water hemlock — which family?
q.e: Apiaceae is a family of mostly aromatic flowering plants named after the type genus Apium, and commonly known as the celery, carrot, or parsley family, or simply as umbellifers.

q.p: This severe blood disorder leaves the bone marrow unable to produce enough red cells, white cells, and platelets, often for no known reason — what is it?
q.e: Aplastic anemia (AA) is a severe hematologic condition in which the body fails to make blood cells in sufficient numbers.

q.p: More than 500 orb-weaving spider species, including the familiar garden spider, belong to this genus first classified in 1757 — which genus?
q.e: Araneus is a genus of common orb-weaving spiders with more than 500 species, among which are the European garden spider and the barn spider.

q.p: This discipline studies past human activity by recovering and analyzing artifacts, architecture, and other material remains through surveying and excavation — name the field?
q.e: Archaeology is the study of human activity through the recovery and analysis of material culture.

q.p: Considered a visual art even though it leans on civil engineering, this discipline gives us cultural symbols that often outlast the civilizations that built them. What is it?
q.e: Architecture is the study and practice of designing structures, especially habitable ones.

q.p: Native to Europe and Asia, which genus of burdock plants owes its seed-dispersal success to burrs that later inspired a famous fastening invention?
q.e: Arctium is a genus of biennial plants commonly known as burdock, family Asteraceae.

q.p: This red giant is the brightest star in the constellation Boötes and the fourth-brightest star in the entire night sky — name the star?
q.e: Arcturus is a red giant star in the northern constellation of Botes, and the brightest star in the constellation.

q.p: Excavated in Argentina starting in 1989 under paleontologist José Bonaparte, this Late Cretaceous titanosaur weighed as much as 80 tons — which genus of giant sauropod?
q.e: Argentinosaurus (meaning "lizard from Argentina") is a genus of giant sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina.

q.p: This amino acid carries a guanidino group that serves as the body's precursor for making nitric oxide, and it's encoded by a generous six codons. Which one is it?
q.e: Arginine is the amino acid with the formula (H2N)(HN)CN(H)(CH2)3CH(NH2)CO2H.

q.p: Which noble gas, symbol Ar and atomic number 18, is the third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere — more plentiful there than carbon dioxide or neon?
q.e: Argon is a chemical element; it has symbol Ar and atomic number 18.

q.p: Named from the Ancient Greek word for silver, this condition results from too much silver exposure and can leave the skin permanently blue-gray — what is it?
q.e: Argyria is a condition caused by excessive exposure to chemical compounds of the element silver, or silver dust.

q.p: Sharing chemistry with phosphorus and antimony, this group-15 metalloid carries the symbol As and a notorious reputation for toxicity — what is it?
q.e: Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.

q.p: Founder of a prominent Russian design studio and an avid, famously foul-mouthed blogger, this designer and entrepreneur is also a member of the Tolstoy family — name this designer?
q.e: Artemy Lebedev (born 13 February 1975) is a Russian designer, entrepreneur and Internet personality.

q.p: This general medical term describes a joint disorder in which the smooth cartilage lining wears away, leaving bone to grind directly on bone during movement — what condition is it?
q.e: Arthritis is a general medical term used to describe a disorder in which the smooth cartilagenous layer that lines a joint is lost, resulting in bone grinding on bone during joint movement.

q.p: Jointed legs, a chitin exoskeleton they must moult to grow, and haemolymph instead of blood mark which wildly diverse group of invertebrates?
q.e: Arthropod are invertebrates in the phylum Arthropoda.

q.p: Named from Greek words for 'even' and 'toe,' this mammal order bears its weight equally on two of its five toes, unlike its odd-toed counterpart — what order is it?
q.e: Artiodactyla (from Ancient Greek rtios 'even' and dktylos 'finger, toe') is an order of placental mammals.

q.p: This medical condition, most often caused in the developed world by liver cirrhosis, is the abnormal buildup of fluid within the abdominal cavity — what is it called?
q.e: Ascites is the abnormal build-up of fluid in the abdomen.

q.p: The second-largest living lizard species after the Komodo dragon, native to South and Southeast Asia. It's a varanid found from India to the Indonesian islands. What is it?
q.e: Asian water monitor (Varanus salvator) is a large varanid lizard native to South and Southeast Asia.

q.p: This genus of roughly 300 evergreen flowering plants includes one edible species enjoyed as a vegetable and another grown purely as an ornamental — which genus?
q.e: Asparagus (genus) is a genus of flowering plants in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Asparagoideae.

q.p: About a third of the several hundred mold species in this genus have a sexual reproductive stage, and some cause infections while others hold commercial value — which genus?
q.e: Aspergillus is a genus consisting of several hundred mold species found in various climates worldwide.

q.p: Doctors reach for this NSAID not just for aches but to treat Kawasaki disease and rheumatic fever — and it's famous for its blood-thinning effect on platelets. What is it?
q.e: Aspirin is the genericized trademark for acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to reduce pain, fever, and inflammation, and as an antithrombotic.

q.p: With atomic number 85 and symbol At, this is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, forming only as a decay product of heavier elements — name it?
q.e: Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.

q.p: First described in 1740, this flowering-plant family rivals only the orchid family in sheer number of species, with over 32,000 recognized today — what family is it?
q.e: Asteraceae is a large family of flowering plants that consists of over 32,000 known species in over 1,900 genera within the order Asterales.

q.p: This common vision condition occurs when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped rather than spherical, causing blurred vision at any distance. What is it?
q.e: Astigmatism is a type of refractive error due to rotational asymmetry in the eye's refractive power.

q.p: Caused by poor circulation, lost nerve supply, or simple disuse, this process shrinks a cell, organ, or tissue below its normal mature size — what's it called?
q.e: Atrophy is the partial or complete wasting away of a part of the body.

q.p: Which genus of early hominins, which lived in Africa during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene, gave rise to the genera Homo, Paranthropus, and Kenyanthropus?
q.e: Australopithecus (-loh-; or, os-, from Latin australis southern 'grc' and (pthkos) ape) is a genus of early hominins that existed in Africa during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene.

q.p: Once native to the highland lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco, this neotenic mole salamander keeps its external gills and stays aquatic for life — what is it?
q.e: Axolotl (from Classical; Ambystoma mexicanum) is a species of mole salamander.

q.p: Part of the family Ericaceae, these shrubs flower in April and May in the Northern Hemisphere and October and November south of the equator — what are they called?
q.e: Azalea (-) are flowering shrubs in the genus Rhododendron, particularly the former subgenera Tsutsusi (evergreen) and Pentanthera (deciduous).

q.p: This American psychologist developed the philosophy of radical behaviorism and pioneered operant conditioning while a longtime professor at Harvard — who is he?
q.e: B. F. Skinner (March 20, 1904 - August 18, 1990) was an American psychologist, behaviorist, inventor, and social philosopher.

q.p: Originally built by Hawker Siddeley and still produced under license in India today, this subsonic British trainer aircraft equips the Red Arrows aerobatic team — which jet?
q.e: BAE Systems Hawk is a British single-engine, subsonic, jet-powered advanced trainer aircraft.

q.p: These large Old World monkeys come in six distinct species, each native to a different region of Africa, with one species also found on the Arabian Peninsula — what primate is it?
q.e: Baboon are primates comprising the genus Papio, one of the 23 genera of Old World monkeys, in the family Cercopithecidae.

q.p: This gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium was the first ever proven experimentally to cause disease, laying the groundwork for germ theory in 1876 — which microbe?
q.e: Bacillus anthracis is a gram-positive and rod-shaped bacterium that causes anthrax, a deadly disease to livestock and, occasionally, to humans.

q.p: Found throughout North America from Canada to northern Mexico, this sea eagle has two subspecies and forms a pair with the white-tailed eagle—name it.
q.e: Bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) is a bird of prey found in North America.

q.p: Technically a giant member of the grass family, this plant's tallest species can grow stalks over 150 feet long and weigh up to 450 kilograms — what plant is it?
q.e: Bamboo are a diverse group of mostly evergreen perennial flowering plants making up the subfamily Bambusoideae of the grass family Poaceae.

q.p: One of the first grains ever domesticated, this cereal crop was cultivated in the Fertile Crescent around 9000 BC and later spread throughout Eurasia by 2000 BC — name the grain?
q.e: Barley (Hordeum vulgare), a member of the grass family, is a major cereal grain grown in temperate climates globally.

q.p: Native to the Mekong and Chao Phraya river basins, this freshwater catfish is marketed in the US as "swai" and in the UK as "river cobbler" — which fish?
q.e: Basa (fish) (Pangasius bocourti), as it is commonly referred to, is a species of primarily freshwater-dwelling catfish in the shark-catfish family, Pangasiidae, native to the Mekong and Chao Phraya river basins of Mainland Southeast Asia.

q.p: The only mammals capable of true sustained flight, members of this order — the second largest among mammals — fly using long digits webbed by a thin membrane. What are they?
q.e: Bat (order Chiroptera) are winged mammals, the only mammals capable of true and sustained flight.

q.p: Only eight species of this stocky-legged, shaggy, short-tailed carnivoran survive, ranging across North and South America and Eurasia — what mammal is it?
q.e: Bear are carnivoran mammals of the family Ursidae.

q.p: This facial hair grows on the jaw, chin, and cheeks, most commonly in adult men, though some women develop it too in a condition called hirsutism — name it?
q.e: Beard is the hair that grows on the jaw, chin, upper lip, lower lip, cheeks, and neck of humans and some non-human animals.

q.p: This large bird of prey is the only known vertebrate whose diet consists mostly — 70 to 90 percent — of bone. What bird is it?
q.e: Bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus), also known as the lammergeier and ossifrage, is a very large bird of prey in the monotypic genus Gypaetus.

q.p: Nicknamed 'Red-Stockings,' this French herding dog breed hails from the plains of Central France — which breed is it?
q.e: Beauceron (French) is a herding dog breed originating from the plains of Central France.

q.p: Which SI unit of radioactivity honors the scientist who co-discovered the phenomenon alongside the Curies?
q.e: Becquerel (symbol: Bq) is the unit of radioactivity in the International System of Units (SI).

q.p: These nocturnal blood-feeding insects from the genus Cimex can trigger skin rashes, itching, and even psychological distress from their bites — what are they commonly called?
q.e: Bed bug are insects from the genus Cimex, which are parasites that feed on blood, usually at night.

q.p: Marketed early on as the Debonair in its conventional-tail form, this piston single has been built continuously longer than any other aircraft ever made — which model?
q.e: Beechcraft Bonanza is an American general aviation aircraft introduced in 1947 by Beech Aircraft Corporation of Wichita, Kansas.

q.p: Grown for its edible taproot in red or golden varieties and closely related to Swiss chard, this vegetable's leaves are eaten too, sold simply as "greens" — which root vegetable?
q.e: Beetroot is the taproot portion of a Beta vulgaris subsp.

q.p: Not contagious and believed to be partly genetic, this multi-system inflammatory condition can also cause blood clots, aneurysms, or blindness in severe cases — which condition?
q.e: Behçet's disease (BD; sometimes written Behcet) is a type of inflammatory disorder which affects multiple parts of the body.

q.p: Coming on over about 48 hours, this temporary one-sided facial paralysis of unknown cause can droop an eyebrow, alter taste, and make sounds painfully loud — what is it?
q.e: Bell's palsy is a type of facial paralysis that results in a temporary inability to control the facial muscles on the affected side of the face.

q.p: The first production aircraft of its type, this American military transport combines vertical takeoff and landing with long-range cruise performance—what is it?
q.e: Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey is an American multi-use, tiltrotor military transport and cargo aircraft with both vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) and short takeoff and landing (STOL) capabilities.

q.p: Native to Europe, this small white-petaled, yellow-centered lawn flower is called 'common,' 'lawn,' or 'English' in various regions — what is its scientific name?
q.e: Bellis perennis (p-), the daisy, is a European species of the family Asteraceae, often considered the archetypal species of the name daisy.

q.p: Six carbons in a flat hexagonal ring, each wearing a single hydrogen — this textbook aromatic hydrocarbon has the formula C6H6 — what is it?
q.e: Benzene is an organic chemical compound with the molecular formula C6H6.

q.p: Designed to replace the aging Tu-126 'Moss,' this Soviet early-warning aircraft saw only about 42 built before the USSR's breakup ended production in 1992 — what is it?
q.e: Beriev A-50 (NATO reporting name: Mainstay) is a Soviet-origin airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft that is based on the Ilyushin Il-76 transport plane.

q.p: A civil-engineering graduate who first reshaped his father's firm toward real estate, this Frenchman now chairs the world's largest luxury goods company — who is he?
q.e: Bernard Arnault (born 5 March 1949) is a French businessman.

q.p: Once chairman of the Nasdaq, this financier admitted to masterminding the largest-known Ponzi scheme in history, estimated at $65 billion — who was he?
q.e: Bernie Madoff (April 29, 1938 - April 14, 2021) was an American financier, con artist, and stock broker who was the admitted mastermind of the largest-known Ponzi scheme in history, worth an estimated $65 billion.

q.p: Native to Southeast Asia, the glossy heart-shaped leaves of this evergreen vine are chewed together with areca nut — name the plant?
q.e: Betel (Piper betle) is a species of flowering plant in the pepper family Piperaceae, native to Southeast Asia.

q.p: Usually the tenth-brightest star in the night sky, this red supergiant in the constellation Orion varies noticeably in brightness over a roughly 400-day cycle — name the star?
q.e: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star in the equatorial constellation of Orion. Its Bayer designation is α Orionis, Latinised to Alpha Orionis and abbreviated Alpha Ori or α Ori.

q.p: Coined in 1814 by chemist William Hyde Wollaston, this polyatomic anion forms as carbonic acid loses a proton, and plays a crucial role buffering the body's pH — what's the ion?
q.e: Bicarbonate (American; nomenclature: hydrogencarbonate) is an intermediate form in the deprotonation of carbonic acid.

q.p: Often called a 'chest cold,' this inflammation of the airways in the lungs typically follows an infection that spreads down from the nose or throat. What condition is it?
q.e: Biceps is a large muscle that lies on the front of the upper arm between the shoulder and the elbow.

q.p: What yellow-green digestive fluid is produced continuously by the liver but stored and concentrated in the gallbladder until it's needed to break down fats in the small intestine?
q.e: Bile (from Latin bilis), also known as gall, is a yellow-green fluid produced by the liver of most vertebrates that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine.

q.p: This red-orange compound, formed from the breakdown of heme, is further processed into pigments that give feces their brown color and urine its straw-yellow hue. What is it?
q.e: Bilirubin (BR) (adopted from German, originally bili, for bile, plus ruber, Latin for red) is a red-orange compound that occurs as the reduction product of biliverdin, a breakdown product of heme.

q.p: From molecules and cells up to whole ecosystems, this science studies living things through ideas like heredity, evolution, and homeostasis — what is it?
q.e: Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms.

q.p: Present in every living cell and abundant in liver and meats, this B vitamin acts as an enzyme cofactor and takes its name from the Greek for 'life' — what is it?
q.e: Biotin (also known as vitamin B7 and vitamin H) is one of the B vitamins - a group of essential dietary micronutrients.

q.p: This brittle, silvery-white post-transition metal can develop a vividly iridescent, rainbow-colored surface from thin-film oxidation when heated. What element is it?
q.e: Bismuth is a chemical element; it has symbol Bi and atomic number 83.

q.p: This colourless industrial compound, easily dissolved in organic solvents but not water, is the key ingredient in most polycarbonate plastics — which chemical?
q.e: Bisphenol A (BPA) is a chemical compound primarily used in the manufacturing of various plastics.

q.p: Represented most commonly as a 1 or a 0, this portmanteau of 'binary digit' is the most fundamental unit of information in computing — what is it called?
q.e: Bit is the most basic unit of information in computing and digital communication.

q.p: So dense that not even light can escape its gravity, this astronomical object's boundary of no return is called the event horizon — name it?
q.e: Black hole is an astronomical body so compact that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping.

q.p: Caused by a recessive allele in the leopard but a dominant one in the jaguar, this dark melanistic variant still secretly carries its usual rosettes — what is it called?
q.e: Black panther is the melanistic colour variant of the leopard (Panthera pardus) and the jaguar (Panthera onca).

q.p: This small bird in the Old World flycatcher family breeds among rocky habitats from the British Isles to Morocco and east to central China — what species is it?
q.e: Black redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros) is a small passerine bird in the Old World flycatcher family.

q.p: A child prodigy who wrote a treatise on conic sections at 16, which Frenchman later traded letters with Fermat on probability and built early calculating machines?
q.e: Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 - 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.

q.p: This insect order contains both cockroaches and termites — the latter now classified as a specialized, social lineage within the former group — what order is it?
q.e: Blattodea is an order of insects that contains cockroaches and termites.

q.p: Around 2,500 species of this insect family defend themselves by secreting a skin-irritating toxin called cantharidin, often flaunting bold warning colors — which family?
q.e: Blister beetle are beetles of the family Meloidae, so called for their defensive secretion of a blistering agent, cantharidin.

q.p: Composed mostly of plasma along with red cells, white cells, and platelets, this body fluid ferries oxygen and nutrients to cells while hauling waste away — name the fluid?
q.e: Blood is a body fluid in the circulatory system of humans and other vertebrates that delivers necessary substances such as nutrients and oxygen to the cells of the body, and transports metabolic waste products away from those same cells.

q.p: Native to North America and introduced to Europe in the 1930s, these prostrate shrubs in the genus Vaccinium range from 4 inches to 13 feet tall — what fruit is it?
q.e: Blueberry are a widely distributed and widespread group of perennial flowering plants with blue or purple berries.

q.p: As Square's chief technology officer, this software engineer helped build Cash App before he was fatally stabbed in San Francisco in 2023 — who was he?
q.e: Bob Lee (businessman) (December 20, 1979 - April 4, 2023) was an American businessman and software engineer who was best known for helping to create the financial service Cash App.

q.p: Recognised by South Africa's Kennel Union but not by the international federation, this large, muscular mastiff-type breed serves as a family guard dog — name it?
q.e: Boerboel is a South African breed of large dog of mastiff type, used as a family guard dog.

q.p: This leafy vegetable forms no head, just green blades atop pale bulbous stalks, with a flavor often compared to a mix of spinach and water chestnut — what vegetable is it?
q.e: Bok choy (American English, Canadian English, and Australian English), pak choi (British English, South African English, and Caribbean English) or pok choi is a type of Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp.

q.p: This rigid, mineralized organ of the vertebrate skeleton produces both red and white blood cells and helps regulate the body's acid-base balance — what is it?
q.e: Bone is a rigid organ that constitutes part of the skeleton in most vertebrate animals.

q.p: Belonging to the Colubridae family of venomous snakes and found only in Sub-Saharan Africa, this reptile's scientific name is Dispholidus typus — what is it commonly called?
q.e: Boomslang (or; Dispholidus typus) is a highly venomous snake in the family Colubridae.

q.p: Native to the Mediterranean and also called 'starflower,' this annual herb's seeds are pressed for oil even though the plant carries mild toxic alkaloids — which plant?
q.e: Borage (or; Borago officinalis), also known as starflower, is an annual herb in the flowering plant family Boraginaceae native to the Mediterranean region.

q.p: What hydrated mineral salt of sodium, mined economically in only a few places worldwide, forms a white crystalline solid that can be dehydrated by heating?
q.e: Borax (also referred to as sodium borate, tincal and tincar) is a salt (ionic compound) normally encountered as a hydrated borate of sodium, with the chemical formula Na2H20B4O17.

q.p: Once known as the Russian Wolfhound until a 1936 name change, this elegant sighthound breed was historically used to hunt wolves — what breed is it?
q.e: Borzoi is a Russian breed of hunting dog of sighthound type.

q.p: Accepted by the American Kennel Club in 1893, this small, compact dog breed with a short tail and erect ears originated in the United States — name the breed?
q.e: Boston Terrier is a breed of dog originating in the United States of America.

q.p: This branch of biology studies how plants have grown, reproduced, and evolved over the last 3.5 billion years of life on Earth — what field is it?
q.e: Botany is the branch of natural science and biology that studies the growth, reproduction and evolution of plants over the last 3.5 billion years of life on earth.

q.p: This family of cloven-hoofed, ruminant mammals includes cattle, bison, buffalo, antelopes, sheep, and goats across 143 living species — name the family?
q.e: Bovidae is the biological family of cloven-hoofed, ruminant mammals that includes cattle, bison, buffalo, antelopes, and goat-antelopes such as sheep and goats.

q.p: Members of this decapod infraorder tuck a tiny tail-like abdomen under a hard thorax and end their front legs in pincers — which true creatures are they?
q.e: Brachyura is an infraorder of decapod crustaceans comprising the true crabs.

q.p: This rhythmic bodily process draws oxygen-rich air into the lungs and expels carbon dioxide, powering the cellular chemistry that turns food into energy — what process is it?
q.e: Breathing (respiring or ventilating) is the rhythmic process of inhaling air into the lungs providing oxygen, and exhaling the air removing carbon dioxide, in the gas exchange process.

q.p: Whose book Atlas of the Heart became an HBO Max documentary series in 2022, following an earlier Netflix film about her work on courage?
q.e: Brené Brown (born November 18, 1965) is an American academic, author and podcaster.

q.p: This American actor played Kyle Parks on Lifetime's The Client List before joining the cast of Revenge as Ben Hunter — who is he?
q.e: Brian Hallisay (born October 31, 1978) is an American actor, known for his roles as Will Davis in The CW drama series Privileged and Kyle Parks in the Lifetime drama series The Client List.

q.p: This outdated 19th-century term for what's now called acute or chronic nephritis was marked by swelling and albumin showing up in the urine — what was it called?
q.e: Bright's disease is a historical classification of kidney diseases that are described in modern medicine as acute or chronic nephritis.

q.p: Formed naturally through evaporation of saline water or generated by salt mining, which concentrated saltwater solution helps de-ice roads and preserve pickled foods?
q.e: Brine (or briny water) is a high-concentration solution of salt (typically sodium chloride or calcium chloride) in water.

q.p: This cabbage-family vegetable, whose large dark-green flowering head is eaten as food, closely resembles its paler relative cauliflower — name it?
q.e: Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var.

q.p: One of only two elements liquid at room temperature, this reddish-brown, pungent-smelling element takes its name from the Greek word for 'stench.' What element is it (symbol Br)?
q.e: Bromine is a chemical element; it has symbol Br and atomic number 35.

q.p: Splitting from the windpipe at the carina into a right and left branch, this airway keeps forking into ever-smaller tubes until it's too narrow for cartilage support — what is it?
q.e: Bronchus (pl.: bronchi) is a passage or airway in the lower respiratory tract that conducts air into the lungs.

q.p: With a mass roughly 13 to 80 times Jupiter's, these substellar objects glow faintly from deuterium fusion rather than true hydrogen burning — what's the term for them?
q.e: Brown dwarf are substellar objects that have more mass than the biggest gas giant planets, but less than the least massive main-sequence stars.

q.p: Also known as undulant fever and Malta fever, this zoonotic illness spreads mainly through drinking unpasteurized milk and is caused by tiny coccobacilli — what is it?
q.e: Brucellosis is a zoonosis (zoonotic disease) spread primarily via ingestion of unpasteurized milk from infected animals.

q.p: Every one of this genus's seven woody species is toxic enough to rival deadly nightshade, and none survive in the wild anymore — only in gardens — which genus?
q.e: Brugmansia is a genus of seven species of flowering plants in the nightshade family Solanaceae.

q.p: This small leafy vegetable, a cultivar of cabbage grown for its edible buds, shares its name with a European capital — what is it?
q.e: Brussels sprout is a member of the Gemmifera cultivar group of cabbages (Brassica oleracea), grown for its edible buds.

q.p: Affecting roughly 22% of people worldwide and often striking during sleep, this parafunctional habit grinds teeth and clenches jaws until enamel wears away — what's it called?
q.e: Bruxism is excessive teeth grinding or jaw clenching.

q.p: This English guard-dog breed combines the size of the Mastiff with genes from the extinct Old English Bulldog, and gained Kennel Club recognition in 1924 — which breed?
q.e: Bullmastiff is an English breed of dog of mastiff type and large size, with a solid build and a short muzzle.

q.p: This flammable, colorless alkane gas with the formula C4H10 takes its name from a Greek word for butter, via butyric acid — what is it?
q.e: Butane is an alkane with the formula C4H10. Butane exists as two isomers, n-butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3 and iso-butane, (CH3)3CH.

q.p: Which winged insect fluttered into the fossil record around 56 million years ago and reaches adulthood only after pupating inside a chrysalis?
q.e: Butterfly are winged insects from the lepidopteran superfamily Papilionoidea, characterised by large, often brightly coloured wings that often fold together when at rest, and a conspicuous, fluttering flight.

q.p: This basic unit of digital information most often consists of eight bits, and is called an 'octet' in network protocol documents to avoid ambiguity. What is it?
q.e: Byte is a unit of digital information that most commonly consists of eight bits.

q.p: Unlike ordinary weight loss from undereating, this illness-linked syndrome strips away muscle mass in ways good nutrition can't fully undo — what condition is it?
q.e: Cachexia is a syndrome that occurs in people with certain illnesses, causing muscle loss that cannot be fully reversed with improved nutrition.

q.p: Its three-dimensional shape mimics adenosine closely enough to plug into the same receptors, blocking the brain's signal to wind down — which psychoactive substance is it?
q.e: Caffeine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant of the methylxanthine class and is the most commonly consumed psychoactive substance globally.

q.p: Atomic number 20 and chemically akin to strontium and barium, this metal is the most common ingredient in limestone — found there as its carbonate. What element?
q.e: Calcium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ca and atomic number 20.

q.p: The very same compound that hardens eggshells, builds pearls, and forms the chalk on a classroom board can also be swallowed as an antacid to calm an upset stomach — what is it?
q.e: Calcium carbonate is a chemical compound with the chemical formula CaCO3.

q.p: Produced when quicklime is mixed with water, this white, powdery compound goes by many names in industry and food prep, where it's labeled E526 — what compound is it?
q.e: Calcium hydroxide (traditionally called slaked lime) is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Ca(OH)2.

q.p: Its common name is a contraction of 'Mary's gold,' honoring the Virgin Mary, but this daisy-family genus's Latin name nods to the calendar instead — which flowering plant?
q.e: Calendula is a genus of about 15-20 species of annual and perennial herbaceous plants in the daisy family, Asteraceae that are often known as marigolds.

q.p: Sole living family in the mammalian suborder Tylopoda, which group unites camels with llamas and their South American relatives?
q.e: Camelidae is a family of mammals belonging to the ungulate order Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates) and the only living family in the suborder Tylopoda.

q.p: Caused by an overgrowth of a common yeast, this fungal infection is known as thrush when it affects the mouth and can also cause a genital yeast infection — name the condition?
q.e: Candidiasis is a fungal infection due to any species of yeasts in the genus Candida or those that were formerly classified in genus Candida but are now classified in the genus Candidozyma.

q.p: This Italian mastiff breed once hunted big game and herded cattle, and today mostly serves as a guard dog and loyal companion — name the breed?
q.e: Cane Corso is an Italian breed of mastiff. It is usually kept as a companion dog or guard dog; it may also be used to protect livestock.

q.p: Discovered in 1940, this non-intoxicating compound extracted from cannabis is used medically as an anticonvulsant for two rare, severe forms of childhood epilepsy — what is it?
q.e: Cannabidiol (CBD) is a phytocannabinoid, one of 113 identified cannabinoids in Cannabis, along with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and accounts for up to 40% of the plant's extract.

q.p: Prized in India for hashish and cultivated from China to West Africa, this Hindu Kush-native plant produces cannabinoid levels well above ordinary hemp — which species?
q.e: Cannabis indica is an annual plant species in the family Cannabaceae indigenous to the Hindu Kush mountains of Southern Asia.

q.p: First classified by Linnaeus in 1753, which herbaceous annual takes its specific name from the Latin for 'cultivated' and has long supplied fiber, seed oil, food and medicine?
q.e: Cannabis sativa is an annual herbaceous flowering plant.

q.p: Bordered by Aquila, Sagittarius, and Aquarius in the sky's watery region, this half-goat, half-fish zodiac figure is the tiniest of the twelve — which constellation?
q.e: Capricornus is one of the constellations of the zodiac.

q.p: Chili peppers likely make this hydrophobic compound to deter hungry mammals and fungi — yet it's exactly what gives them their burning, pungent heat. What is it?
q.e: Capsaicin (8-methyl-N-vanillyl-6-nonenamide) (commonly) is a toxin that is the main active component of chili peppers and gives them their distinct pungent, "spicy" or "hot" taste.

q.p: Domesticated roughly 6,000 years ago in Mexico, this nightshade produces berries in red, green, and yellow ranging from mild to fiery — what is its scientific name?
q.e: Capsicum annuum is a flowering plant in the family Solanaceae (nightshades), native to the northern regions of South America and to southwestern North America.

q.p: Native to nearly all of South America, this semiaquatic, grass-munching cousin of the guinea pig holds the title of largest living rodent — what is it?
q.e: Capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) is the largest living rodent, native to all countries in South America except Chile.

q.p: Standardized worldwide in 1907 as exactly 200 milligrams, this unit of mass is used to weigh gemstones and pearls, and is divisible into 100 smaller 'points' — what unit is it?
q.e: Carat (mass) (ct) is a unit of mass equal to 200 mg (0.00705 oz; 0.00643 ozt), which is used for measuring gemstones and pearls.

q.p: Also called meridian fennel, this biennial plant in the carrot family is native to western Asia, Europe, and North Africa — name it?
q.e: Caraway (Carum carvi), also known as meridian fennel, is a biennial plant in the family Apiaceae, native to western Asia, Europe, and North Africa.

q.p: Its name comes from the Latin for "coal," and one of its isotopes decays with a 5,700-year half-life that lets scientists date ancient remains — which element is it?
q.e: Carbon (from Latin carbo 'coal') is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.

q.p: This medical specialty diagnoses and treats congenital heart defects, valvular disease, and heart failure, and is a sub-specialty of internal medicine — which field?
q.e: Cardiology (from Ancient Greek (kardi) 'heart' and - (-logia) 'study') is the study of the heart.

q.p: Seen as the frontman of Mexican neoliberalism, this economist-president championed and signed NAFTA after an election clouded by fraud accusations — who is he?
q.e: Carlos Salinas de Gortari (Spanish; born 3 April 1948) is a Mexican economist and former politician who served as the 60th president of Mexico from 1988 to 1994.

q.p: Which Mediterranean evergreen tree, grown mainly in Spain, produces edible seed pods often ground into a chocolate substitute, with seeds that yield a gum used as a food thickener?
q.e: Carob (Ceratonia siliqua) is a flowering evergreen tree or shrub in the Caesalpinioideae subfamily of the legume family, Fabaceae.

q.p: This root vegetable owes its typical orange color to beta-carotene, though heirloom varieties can be white, purple, or even black — what vegetable is it?
q.e: Carrot (Daucus carota subsp.

q.p: Combining science, aesthetics, and technique, this field is the study and practice of making and using maps to communicate spatial information — what field is it?
q.e:
Cartography is the study and practice of making and using maps. The fundamental objectives of traditional cartography are to:

Set the map's agenda and select traits of the object to be mapped.

q.p: Portuguese explorers carried this tropical American tree to India in the 16th century; today Ivory Coast and India lead a 3.9-million-ton global harvest of its nut — what is it?
q.e: Cashew is the common name of a tropical evergreen tree Anacardium occidentale, in the family Anacardiaceae.

q.p: Which metabolic process is the polar opposite of anabolism, breaking large molecules such as proteins and lipids down into monomers while releasing energy, some of it lost as heat?
q.e: Catabolism is the set of metabolic pathways that breaks down molecules into smaller units that are either oxidized to release energy or used in other anabolic reactions.

q.p: Belonging to the trumpet-vine family Bignoniaceae, this tree genus thrives across warm parts of North America, the Caribbean, and East Asia — what is it called?
q.e: Catalpa is a genus of flowering plants in the family Bignoniaceae, native to warm temperate and subtropical regions of North America, the Caribbean, and East Asia.

q.p: This neuropsychiatric syndrome, often linked to mood or psychotic disorders, can leave a person nearly motionless for days or cause repetitive, purposeless movements. What is it?
q.e: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome most commonly seen in people with underlying mood disorders such as major depressive disorder, or psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia.

q.p: A first-generation cephalosporin that can be swallowed rather than infused, this antibiotic disrupts the bacterial cell wall to treat ear, skin and urinary infections — what is it?
q.e: Cefalexin is an antibiotic that can treat a number of bacterial infections. It kills gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria by disrupting the growth of the bacterial cell wall.

q.p: Retired from Istanbul Technical University, this geologist holds foreign membership in both the US and Russian National Academies of Sciences. Who is he?
q.e: Celâl Şengör (born 24 March 1955) is a Turkish geologist.

q.p: Sporting one pair of legs per body segment, this venomous arthropod always has an odd number of leg pairs — anywhere from 15 to 191 — what is it?
q.e: Centipede (from Neo-Latin centi- 'hundred' and Latin pes, pedis 'foot') are predatory arthropods belonging to the class Chilopoda of the subphylum Myriapoda, an arthropod group which includes millipedes and other multi-legged animals.

q.p: Their name is Greek for "head-feet," and fishers sometimes call them "inkfish" for their ink-squirting trick; squid, octopus and nautilus all belong. What's this molluscan class?
q.e: Cephalopod is any member of the molluscan class Cephalopoda (Greek plural, kephalpodes; "head-feet") such as a squid, octopus, cuttlefish, or nautilus.

q.p: This worldwide family of over 5,000 fly species — found everywhere except the Antarctic and Arctic — includes the biting midges also known as sand flies — what is it called?
q.e: Ceratopogonidae is a family of flies colloquially known as no-see-ums, sand flies, or biting midges, generally 1-3 millimetres (116-18 in) in length.

q.p: In calculus, this formula lets you find the derivative of a composed function h(x) = z(y(x)) using the derivatives of z and y separately — what is it called?
q.e: Chain rule is a formula that expresses the derivative of the composition of two differentiable functions z and y in terms of the derivatives of z and y.

q.p: Also known by the taxonomic synonym Epilobium, this hardy perennial in the willowherb family is native throughout the temperate north — which plant?
q.e: Chamaenerion angustifolium is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the willowherb family, Onagraceae.

q.p: Famous for color-shifting camouflage and zygodactylous, pincer-like feet, which family of roughly 200 Old World lizard species is this?
q.e: Chameleon (family Chamaeleonidae) are a distinctive and highly specialized clade of Old World lizards with 200 species described as of June 2015.

q.p: Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like plant is a staple in calming herbal tea, beer brewing, and even garden ground cover — what is it?
q.e: Chamomile (American English) or camomile (British English; see spelling differences) (or) is the common name for several daisy-like plants of the family Asteraceae.

q.p: First flown in 1998, this Chinese-built multirole combat aircraft features a delta wing and canard design and is nicknamed "Vigorous Dragon" — which fighter jet is it?
q.e: Chengdu J-10 (pinyin: Jian-Shi), also known as Menglong (pinyin: Menglong; lit. 'Vigorous Dragon'), is a Chinese medium-weight, single-engine, multirole combat aircraft with a delta wing and canard design.

q.p: Built under license from the Soviet MiG-21, this Chinese fighter jet carries the NATO reporting name Fishcan and specializes in short-range air combat — what aircraft is it?
q.e: Chengdu J-7 (pinyin: Jin-7; third generation export version J-7; NATO reporting name: Fishcan) is a Chinese fighter aircraft.

q.p: Sometimes called melde or wild spinach, this weedy annual plant is often distinguished from its relatives in the same genus as the 'white' goosefoot — which plant?
